modules.name: char
modules.doc:
Unicode character type extensions.

This module provides additional methods for working with Unicode characters
beyond what `core::char` provides. It focuses on Unicode-specific properties
and General Category classification.

# Relationship with `core::char`

The `core::char` module provides the primary `Char` type and common
character operations. This module (`core::unicode::char`) extends that
with Unicode-specific functionality:

- General Category classification (`is_letter`, `is_mark`, `is_symbol`, etc.)
- Surrogate detection (`is_surrogate`, `is_high_surrogate`, `is_low_surrogate`)
- Grapheme extend property (`is_grapheme_extend`)

For basic character operations, prefer using `core::char` directly.

# Examples

```tml
use core::char          // Primary char operations
use core::unicode::char // Extended Unicode properties

let c: Char = 0x03B1  // Greek alpha 'α'

// Use core::char for basic operations
assert(core::char::is_alphabetic(c))
assert(core::char::is_lowercase(c))

// Use core::unicode::char for Unicode-specific operations
assert(unicode::char::is_letter(c))
let cat = unicode::char::general_category(c)
```

items.name: BOM
items.doc:
The byte order mark (BOM): U+FEFF

The BOM is used at the start of a text stream to indicate:
- The byte order (endianness) of the text
- That the text is Unicode
items.summary: The byte order mark (BOM): U+FEFF

items.name: ZWNBSP
items.doc:
Zero Width No-Break Space (ZWNBSP): U+FEFF

This is the same code point as BOM, but used inline as a word joiner.
Note: U+2060 WORD JOINER is now preferred for this use.
items.summary: Zero Width No-Break Space (ZWNBSP): U+FEFF

items.name: ZERO_WIDTH_SPACE
items.doc: Zero Width Space: U+200B
items.summary: Zero Width Space: U+200B

items.name: ZWNJ
items.doc: Zero Width Non-Joiner: U+200C
items.summary: Zero Width Non-Joiner: U+200C

items.name: ZWJ
items.doc: Zero Width Joiner: U+200D
items.summary: Zero Width Joiner: U+200D

items.name: is_high_surrogate
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the value is a high (leading) surrogate (0xD800-0xDBFF).

High surrogates are the first code unit in a UTF-16 surrogate pair.
They are not valid Unicode scalar values on their own.
items.summary: Returns `true` if the value is a high (leading) surrogate (0xD800-0xDBFF).

items.name: is_low_surrogate
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the value is a low (trailing) surrogate (0xDC00-0xDFFF).

Low surrogates are the second code unit in a UTF-16 surrogate pair.
They are not valid Unicode scalar values on their own.
items.summary: Returns `true` if the value is a low (trailing) surrogate (0xDC00-0xDFFF).

items.name: is_surrogate
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the value is any surrogate (0xD800-0xDFFF).

Surrogates are reserved for UTF-16 encoding and are not valid
Unicode scalar values.
items.summary: Returns `true` if the value is any surrogate (0xD800-0xDFFF).

items.name: is_grapheme_extend
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is a grapheme extending character.

Grapheme extending characters are combining marks that extend the
previous base character (like accents, diacritics). They don't form
independent grapheme clusters.

# Examples

```tml
// Combining acute accent
assert(is_grapheme_extend(0x0301))

// Regular letter
assert(not is_grapheme_extend('a' as Char))
```
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is a grapheme extending character.

items.name: is_cased
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character has the Cased property.

A character is cased if it has different uppercase and lowercase forms,
or is defined as cased by Unicode.

# Examples

```tml
assert(is_cased('a' as Char))
assert(is_cased('A' as Char))
assert(not is_cased('1' as Char))
assert(not is_cased('中' as Char))
```
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character has the Cased property.

items.name: is_format
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is a format control character.

Format characters (Unicode category Cf) are invisible characters
that affect text processing, such as:
- Zero-width spaces and joiners
- Bidirectional formatting marks
- Soft hyphens
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is a format control character.

items.name: is_private_use
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is a private use character.

Private use characters are reserved for application-specific use
and have no standard meaning in Unicode.
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is a private use character.

items.name: is_unassigned
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is unassigned in Unicode.

Unassigned characters are code points that have not been given
a meaning in the current Unicode version.
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is unassigned in Unicode.

items.name: to_titlecase
items.doc:
Converts the character to titlecase.

For most characters, titlecase is the same as uppercase.
However, some characters have distinct titlecase forms:
- Croatian/Serbian digraphs: ǆ → Ǆ (not ǅ), but titlecase is Ǆ → ǅ
- Ligatures: ﬁ → Fi (titlecase) vs FI (uppercase)

# Examples

```tml
assert_eq(to_titlecase('a' as Char), 'A' as Char)
assert_eq(to_titlecase(0x01C6), 0x01C5)  // ǆ → ǅ
```
items.summary: Converts the character to titlecase.

items.name: eq_ignore_case
items.signature: func eq_ignore_case(a: Char, b: Char) -> Bool
items.doc:
Compares two characters case-insensitively using Unicode case folding.

This performs full Unicode case-insensitive comparison, unlike
`core::char::eq_ignore_ascii_case` which only handles ASCII.

# Examples

```tml
assert(eq_ignore_case('A' as Char, 'a' as Char))
assert(eq_ignore_case('Σ' as Char, 'σ' as Char))  // Greek sigma
assert(eq_ignore_case('ß' as Char, 'ẞ' as Char))  // German sharp s
```
items.summary: Compares two characters case-insensitively using Unicode case folding.

items.name: general_category
items.doc:
Returns the Unicode General Category for this character.

Every Unicode character belongs to exactly one General Category.
See [`GeneralCategory`] for the full list of categories.

# Examples

```tml
use core::unicode::GeneralCategory

assert_eq(general_category('A' as Char), UppercaseLetter)
assert_eq(general_category('a' as Char), LowercaseLetter)
assert_eq(general_category('5' as Char), DecimalNumber)
```
items.summary: Returns the Unicode General Category for this character.

items.name: is_letter
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is in the Letter category (L).

This includes:
- Uppercase letters (Lu)
- Lowercase letters (Ll)
- Titlecase letters (Lt)
- Modifier letters (Lm)
- Other letters (Lo) - includes CJK ideographs
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is in the Letter category (L).

items.name: is_mark
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is in the Mark category (M).

Marks are combining characters that attach to base characters.
This includes:
- Nonspacing marks (Mn) - accents, diacritics
- Spacing combining marks (Mc)
- Enclosing marks (Me)
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is in the Mark category (M).

items.name: is_number
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is in the Number category (N).

This includes:
- Decimal digits (Nd) - 0-9 and digits from other scripts
- Letter numbers (Nl) - Roman numerals
- Other numbers (No) - fractions, subscripts, etc.
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is in the Number category (N).

items.name: is_punctuation
items.doc: Returns `true` if the character is in the Punctuation category (P).
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is in the Punctuation category (P).

items.name: is_symbol
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is in the Symbol category (S).

This includes:
- Math symbols (Sm) - +, -, =, etc.
- Currency symbols (Sc) - $, €, ¥, etc.
- Modifier symbols (Sk) - ^, `, etc.
- Other symbols (So) - emoji, dingbats, etc.
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is in the Symbol category (S).

items.name: is_separator
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is in the Separator category (Z).

This includes:
- Space separators (Zs) - various space characters
- Line separators (Zl) - U+2028
- Paragraph separators (Zp) - U+2029
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is in the Separator category (Z).

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
Unicode character operations and classification.

This module provides Unicode-aware character classification and property
lookup functions, complementing the ASCII-specific functions in `core::ascii`.

# Unicode Version

The Unicode data in this module corresponds to Unicode version 15.1.0.
New versions of Unicode are released regularly, and this module may be
updated to reflect newer standards.

# Main Components

- [`UNICODE_VERSION`]: The Unicode standard version this implementation follows
- [`Char`]: Extension methods for Unicode characters (represented as U32)
- Character classification functions (alphabetic, numeric, whitespace, etc.)
- Case conversion utilities

# Examples

```tml
use core::unicode

// Check if a character is alphabetic (works with non-ASCII)
assert(unicode::is_alphabetic('α' as U32))  // Greek alpha
assert(unicode::is_alphabetic('中' as U32))  // Chinese character

// Case conversion
let upper = unicode::to_uppercase('é' as U32)
assert_eq(upper, 'É' as U32)
```

items.name: is_alphabetic
items.doc:
The version of Unicode that this implementation is based on.

This constant allows code to check which Unicode standard version
underlies the character classification and conversion methods.

The version is represented as a tuple of (major, minor, patch).

# Examples

```tml
use core::unicode::UNICODE_VERSION

let (major, minor, patch) = UNICODE_VERSION
println("Unicode version: {major}.{minor}.{patch}")
```
Returns `true` if the character is alphabetic according to Unicode.

This includes letters from all scripts (Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, CJK, etc.)
as well as letter modifiers and marks.

# Examples

```tml
assert(is_alphabetic('a' as U32))
assert(is_alphabetic('Σ' as U32))   // Greek Sigma
assert(is_alphabetic('日' as U32))  // Japanese
assert(not is_alphabetic('5' as U32))
```
items.summary: The version of Unicode that this implementation is based on.

items.name: is_lowercase
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is lowercase.

This is true for lowercase letters in all scripts that distinguish case.

# Examples

```tml
assert(is_lowercase('a' as U32))
assert(is_lowercase('ω' as U32))   // Greek omega
assert(not is_lowercase('A' as U32))
```
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is lowercase.

items.name: is_uppercase
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is uppercase.

This is true for uppercase letters in all scripts that distinguish case.

# Examples

```tml
assert(is_uppercase('A' as U32))
assert(is_uppercase('Ω' as U32))   // Greek Omega
assert(not is_uppercase('a' as U32))
```
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is uppercase.

items.name: is_numeric
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is numeric.

This includes decimal digits (0-9), as well as numeric characters from
other scripts and Roman numerals.

# Examples

```tml
assert(is_numeric('5' as U32))
assert(is_numeric('٤' as U32))   // Arabic-Indic 4
assert(is_numeric('Ⅳ' as U32))  // Roman numeral 4
assert(not is_numeric('a' as U32))
```
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is numeric.

items.name: is_alphanumeric
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is alphanumeric.

This is equivalent to `is_alphabetic(c) or is_numeric(c)`.
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is alphanumeric.

items.name: is_whitespace
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is whitespace according to Unicode.

This includes ASCII whitespace as well as Unicode-specific whitespace
characters like non-breaking space, em space, etc.

# Examples

```tml
assert(is_whitespace(' ' as U32))    // Regular space
assert(is_whitespace('\t' as U32))   // Tab
assert(is_whitespace(0x00A0))         // Non-breaking space
assert(is_whitespace(0x2003))         // Em space
```
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is whitespace according to Unicode.

items.name: is_control
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is a control character.

Control characters are non-printing characters that affect text processing.
This includes ASCII control characters (0x00-0x1F, 0x7F) and Unicode
control characters in the Cc category.
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is a control character.

items.name: is_grapheme_extend
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character has grapheme extend property.

Grapheme extending characters are combining marks that extend the
previous base character (like accents, diacritics).
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character has grapheme extend property.

items.name: is_valid_scalar
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is a valid Unicode scalar value.

Valid scalar values are in range 0x0000-0xD7FF and 0xE000-0x10FFFF.
The range 0xD800-0xDFFF is reserved for UTF-16 surrogates.
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is a valid Unicode scalar value.

items.name: is_printable
items.doc:
Returns `true` if the character is printable.

A character is printable if it has a visual representation (including space).
Control characters and unassigned code points are not printable.
items.summary: Returns `true` if the character is printable.

items.name: to_uppercase
items.doc:
Converts a character to its uppercase equivalent.

If the character has no uppercase equivalent, returns the character unchanged.
Some characters may map to multiple characters; this function returns only
the simple (single character) mapping.

# Examples

```tml
assert_eq(to_uppercase('a' as U32), 'A' as U32)
assert_eq(to_uppercase('ß' as U32), 'ẞ' as U32)  // German sharp S
assert_eq(to_uppercase('5' as U32), '5' as U32)  // No change
```
items.summary: Converts a character to its uppercase equivalent.

items.name: to_lowercase
items.doc:
Converts a character to its lowercase equivalent.

If the character has no lowercase equivalent, returns the character unchanged.

# Examples

```tml
assert_eq(to_lowercase('A' as U32), 'a' as U32)
assert_eq(to_lowercase('Σ' as U32), 'σ' as U32)  // Greek Sigma
assert_eq(to_lowercase('5' as U32), '5' as U32)  // No change
```
items.summary: Converts a character to its lowercase equivalent.

items.name: to_titlecase
items.doc:
Converts a character to its titlecase equivalent.

For most characters, titlecase is the same as uppercase.
Some characters (like 'ǆ') have distinct titlecase forms ('ǅ').
items.summary: Converts a character to its titlecase equivalent.

items.name: GeneralCategory
items.doc:
Unicode General Category

Each Unicode character is assigned to exactly one General Category.
Categories are grouped into major classes:
- L: Letter (Lu, Ll, Lt, Lm, Lo)
- M: Mark (Mn, Mc, Me)
- N: Number (Nd, Nl, No)
- P: Punctuation (Pc, Pd, Ps, Pe, Pi, Pf, Po)
- S: Symbol (Sm, Sc, Sk, So)
- Z: Separator (Zs, Zl, Zp)
- C: Other (Cc, Cf, Cs, Co, Cn)
items.summary: Unicode General Category

items.name: general_category
items.doc:
Returns the Unicode General Category for a character.

# Examples

```tml
let cat = general_category('A' as U32)
assert_eq(cat, UppercaseLetter)
```

Unicode property tables and lookup functions.

This module contains the data tables and lookup functions for Unicode
character properties. The data is derived from the Unicode Character
Database (UCD) version 15.1.0.

The tables use a combination of techniques for space efficiency:
- Range-based lookup for contiguous blocks
- Binary search for sparse properties
- Two-stage tables for common properties

This module is internal and not intended for direct use.
Use the functions in `core::unicode` instead.

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
PostgreSQL driver for the TML database abstraction layer.

Self-contained package with libpq FFI bindings, connection adapter,
prepared statement support, and PostgreSQL-specific dialect.

# Quick start

```tml
use postgresql::connection::PgConnection

let conn = PgConnection::connect("host=localhost dbname=mydb")!
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE t (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, val TEXT)")!
conn.execute("INSERT INTO t (val) VALUES ('hello')")!
```

# Module structure

- [`ffi`] — Raw libpq C function bindings (low-level)
- [`connection`] — `PgConnection` implementing `Connection` behavior
- [`statement`] — `PgStatement` implementing `PreparedStatement` behavior
- [`dialect`] — `PostgresDialect` implementing `Dialect` behavior
- [`driver`] — `PgDriver` marker type
- [`types`] — PostgreSQL OID-to-ColumnType mapping
modules.summary: PostgreSQL driver for the TML database abstraction layer.

modules.name: statement
modules.doc:
PostgreSQL prepared statement adapter.

[`PgStatement`] wraps a named prepared statement on a libpq connection
and implements the [`PreparedStatement`] behavior for database-agnostic
usage.

# Lifecycle

1. Create via `PgStatement::prepare(conn_handle, sql, param_count)`
2. Bind parameters with `bind_*` methods (1-based index)
3. Execute with `run()` (for DML) or `execute_query()` + `step()` + `column_*` (for queries)
4. Call `reset()` to re-execute with new parameter bindings
5. Call `finalize()` when done (deallocates the server-side statement)

# Examples

```tml
let stmt = PgStatement::prepare(conn.raw_handle(), "SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE age > $1", 1)!
stmt.bind_i64(1, 25)!
stmt.execute_query()!
loop (stmt.step()) {
    let id = stmt.column_i64(0)
    let name = stmt.column_str(1)
    println(name)
}
stmt.finalize()
```

items.name: PgStatement
items.doc:
A prepared SQL statement backed by PostgreSQL via libpq.

Each `PgStatement` corresponds to a named prepared statement on the
server.  Parameters are bound as text strings (PostgreSQL text protocol),
and results are fetched in text format.

The statement holds a reference to the connection handle (borrowed, not
owned).  The connection must remain open for the lifetime of the statement.
items.summary: A prepared SQL statement backed by PostgreSQL via libpq.

methods.name: prepare
methods.signature: func prepare(conn_handle: ptr Unit, sql: Str, param_count: I32) -> Outcome[PgStatement, DbError]
methods.doc:
Prepares a SQL statement on the given connection.

`conn_handle` is a raw `PGconn*` pointer (obtain via
`PgConnection::raw_handle()`).

`sql` is the query text with `$1`, `$2`, ... placeholders.

`param_count` is the number of parameters in the query.

# Errors

modules.name: event_loop
modules.doc:
Single-threaded event loop for async I/O.

Integrates I/O polling (Poller) + timers (TimerWheel) + callbacks.
Node.js-style architecture: one event loop per thread.

# Examples

```tml
use std::aio::event_loop::EventLoop
use std::time::Instant

let mut loop: EventLoop = EventLoop::new()
let token: U32 = loop.register(socket_handle, READABLE)
loop.on_readable(token, callback_fn as I64)
loop.run()
loop.destroy()
```

modules.name: timer_wheel
modules.doc:
Hashed timer wheel for efficient timeout management.

Two-level timer wheel with O(1) insert, cancel, and fire.
Level 0: 64 slots × 1ms = 0-63ms (fine-grained)
Level 1: 64 slots × 64ms = 64ms-4095ms (coarse-grained)
Timers >4096ms go into an overflow list, re-inserted on advance.

Inspired by tokio's timer wheel and Varghese & Lauck's paper.

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
Specialized memory allocators and layout utilities.

This module re-exports allocator types from `core` under a unified
namespace. The canonical definitions live in `core::arena`, `core::pool`,
`core::cache`, and `core::soo`.

# Modules

| Module | Description | Canonical |
|--------|-------------|-----------|
| [`arena`] | Bump-pointer arena allocator | `core::arena` |
| [`pool`] | Lock-free object pool | `core::pool` |
| [`cache`] | Cache-line aligned storage | `core::cache` |
| [`soo`] | Small object optimization | `core::soo` |

# When to Use

- **Arena**: Many small, short-lived allocations freed together (parsers, ASTs)
- **Pool**: Reuse objects to avoid allocation overhead (connection pools, buffers)
- **Cache**: Performance-critical data that must avoid false sharing
- **SOO**: Small collections that usually fit inline (< 8 elements)

modules.name: behaviors
modules.doc:
Behavior implementations for collection types.

This module provides behavior implementations for the collection types
[`List[T]`] and [`HashMap[K, V]`] defined in this crate.

# List[T] Implementations

[`List`] implements the following behaviors:

| Behavior | Constraint | Description |
|----------|------------|-------------|
| [`Duplicate`] | `T: Duplicate` | Deep clone of the list |
| [`PartialEq`] | `T: PartialEq` | Equality comparison |
| [`Eq`] | `T: Eq` | Reflexive equality |
| [`PartialOrd`] | `T: PartialOrd` | Lexicographic ordering |
| [`Ord`] | `T: Ord` | Total lexicographic ordering |
| [`Default`] | - | Creates empty list |
| [`Display`] | `T: Display` | String representation |
| [`Debug`] | `T: Debug` | Debug representation |
| [`Hash`] | `T: Hash` | Hash of all elements |
| [`Index`] | - | Index access with `list[i]` |
| [`FromIterator`] | - | Build from iterator |
| [`IntoIterator`] | - | Iterate over elements |

# HashMap[K, V] Implementations

[`HashMap`] implements:

| Behavior | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| [`Default`] | Creates empty map |
| [`Display`] | String representation |
| [`Debug`] | Debug representation |
| [`Index`] | Key access with `map[key]` |

# Examples

## List Operations

```tml
use std::collections::List

let list = List::from([1, 2, 3])

// Equality
assert(list == List::from([1, 2, 3]))

// Ordering (lexicographic)
assert(List::from([1, 2]) < List::from([1, 3]))

// Display
println(list.to_string())  // "[1, 2, 3]"

// Iteration
for item in list {
    println(item.to_string())
}
```

## HashMap Operations

```tml
use std::collections::HashMap

let map: HashMap[Str, I64] = HashMap::default()
map.insert("key", 42)

// Index access
let value = map["key"]  // 42
```

Lexicographic ordering for lists.

Lists are compared element by element from the start. The first differing
element determines the ordering. If all compared elements are equal, the
shorter list is considered "less than" the longer one.

modules.doc:
Sorted key-value map backed by sorted arrays with binary search.

`BTreeMap[K, V]` maintains keys in sorted order, providing O(log n) lookup,
O(n) insertion (due to shifting), and ordered iteration.

# Example

```tml
use std::collections::BTreeMap

var m: BTreeMap[I64, I64] = BTreeMap[I64, I64]::new()
m.insert(3, 30)
m.insert(1, 10)
m.insert(2, 20)
let v: I64 = m.get(2)  // 20
```
modules.summary: Sorted key-value map backed by sorted arrays with binary search.

modules.name: buffer
modules.doc:
Byte buffer for binary data manipulation — pure TML implementation.

`Buffer` provides efficient byte-level I/O operations for
serialization, network protocols, and binary file handling.
Compatible with Node.js Buffer API.

# Memory Layout

```
Header (32 bytes at handle):
  offset 0:  data (*Unit) — pointer to byte array
  offset 8:  len (I64)   — number of bytes written
  offset 16: capacity (I64) — allocated size
  offset 24: read_pos (I64) — current read position
```

# Example

```tml
let buf = Buffer::new(64)
buf.write_i32(42)
buf.write_i64(123456789)
buf.reset_read()
let num = buf.read_i32()  // 42
buf.destroy()
```

modules.name: class_collections
modules.doc:
Collection types for common data structures.

This module provides collection types following standard patterns.

# Types

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`ArrayList[T]`] | Dynamic array with indexed access |
| [`HashSet[T]`] | Hash-based set for unique elements |
| [`Queue[T]`] | FIFO queue |
| [`Stack[T]`] | LIFO stack |
| [`LinkedList[T]`] | Doubly-linked list |

```tml
use std::collections::class_collections::*

let list: ArrayList[I32] = ArrayList::create[I32]()
list.add(1)
list.add(2)
list.add(3)
print(list.count().to_string())  // 3
```

modules.name: hashmap
modules.doc:
Hash-based key-value collection type — pure TML implementation.

`HashMap[K, V]` stores key-value pairs with O(1) average lookup time.
Uses open-addressing with linear probing, FNV-1a hashing, and Swiss Table-style
control bytes for fast probe filtering.

Keys and values are stored internally as I64 (type-erased).
Hashing uses K's `Hash` impl (content-based for Str, value-based for integers).
Key comparison uses K's `==` operator (strcmp for Str, value equality for integers).

# Example

```tml
let scores = HashMap[Str, I32]::new(16)
scores.set("Alice", 100)
scores.set("Bob", 85)
let alice_score = scores.get("Alice")  // 100
scores.destroy()
```
modules.summary: Hash-based key-value collection type — pure TML implementation.

Dynamic array collection type — pure TML implementation.

`List[T]` is a generic collection that stores elements of type `T`
contiguously in memory and grows as needed.

Elements are stored at their natural size using `size_of[T]()`.
This correctly handles scalar types (I32, I64, Str) as well as
multi-field struct types (LinkedListNode, Bm25Result, etc.).

# Example

```tml
let nums = List[I32]::new(8)
nums.push(10)

let first = nums.get(0)  // 10
nums.destroy()
```

modules.name: mod

Collection types for TML programs.

This module provides generic collection types for storing and
manipulating groups of elements.

# Runtime-backed Types (C — migration targets)

These types are backed by the C runtime and will be migrated to pure TML.
They work today but carry C-runtime debt. See ROADMAP.md Phase 4.

| Type | Description | Pure TML replacement |
|------|-------------|---------------------|
| [`List[T]`] | Dynamic array | `ArrayList[T]` |
| [`HashMap[K, V]`] | Hash table (I64 keys) | (planned) |
| [`Buffer`] | Byte buffer | (planned) |

# Pure TML Types (preferred for new code)

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`ArrayList[T]`] | Dynamic array with indexed access |
| [`HashSet[T]`] | Hash-based set for unique elements |
| [`Queue[T]`] | FIFO queue |
| [`Stack[T]`] | LIFO stack |
| [`LinkedList[T]`] | Doubly-linked list |
| [`Deque[T]`] | Double-ended queue |
| [`BTreeMap[K, V]`] | Sorted key-value map |

modules.name: console
modules.doc:
Developer console utilities for debugging and profiling.

Provides a simple, unstructured logging API similar to JavaScript's
`console` object. For production logging with levels and filtering,
use [`std::log`] instead.

# Functions

| Category | Functions |
|----------|-----------|
| Output   | `log`, `warn`, `error`, `debug`, `trace` |
| Timing   | `time`, `time_end` |
| Counting | `count`, `count_reset` |
| Grouping | `group`, `group_end` |
| Assert   | `assert` |
| Display  | `table` |

# Examples

```tml
use std::console

console::log("hello world")
console::warn("this might be a problem")
console::error("something went wrong")

console::time("operation")
// ... do work ...
console::time_end("operation")  // prints: operation: 42ms

console::count("loop")  // prints: loop: 1
console::count("loop")  // prints: loop: 2
console::count_reset("loop")

console::group("Section")
console::log("indented message")
console::group_end()
```
modules.summary: Developer console utilities for debugging and profiling.

items.name: log
items.doc:
Print a message to stdout.

The simplest console output function. Messages are prefixed with
the current indentation level (set by `group`/`group_end`).

# Examples

```tml
console::log("Server started on port 8080")
```
items.summary: Print a message to stdout.

items.name: warn
items.doc:
Print a warning message to stdout.

Prefixes the message with `[WARN]` to distinguish it from
normal log output.

# Examples

```tml
console::warn("Connection pool is 80% full")
```
items.summary: Print a warning message to stdout.

items.name: error
items.doc:
Print an error message to stdout.

Prefixes the message with `[ERROR]` to indicate a problem.

# Examples

```tml
console::error("Failed to connect to database")
```
items.summary: Print an error message to stdout.

items.name: debug
items.doc:
Print a debug message to stdout.

Prefixes the message with `[DEBUG]` for development-time
diagnostic output.

# Examples

```tml
console::debug("Cache miss for key: users")
```
items.summary: Print a debug message to stdout.

items.name: trace
items.doc:
Print a trace message to stdout.

Prefixes the message with `[TRACE]` for fine-grained tracing
of program execution.

# Examples

```tml
console::trace("Entering parse_expression()")
```
items.summary: Print a trace message to stdout.

items.name: time
items.doc:
Start a named timer.

Records the current monotonic time under the given label.
Call `time_end` with the same label to print the elapsed time.
If a timer with the same label already exists, it is restarted.

# Examples

```tml
console::time("database_query")
// ... perform query ...
console::time_end("database_query")  // prints: database_query: 127ms
```
items.summary: Start a named timer.

items.name: time_end
items.doc:
Stop a named timer and print the elapsed time.

Looks up the timer started with `time(label)`, computes the
elapsed duration, and prints it in milliseconds. If no timer
with the given label exists, prints a warning instead.

# Examples

```tml
console::time("parse")
// ... do work ...
console::time_end("parse")  // prints: parse: 3ms
```
items.summary: Stop a named timer and print the elapsed time.

items.name: count
items.doc:
Increment and print a named counter.

Each call increments the counter for the given label by 1 and
prints the current count. The counter starts at 1 on first call.
Use `count_reset` to reset a counter to 0.

# Examples

```tml
console::count("requests")  // prints: requests: 1
console::count("requests")  // prints: requests: 2
console::count("requests")  // prints: requests: 3
```
items.summary: Increment and print a named counter.

items.name: count_reset
items.doc:
Reset a named counter to 0.

After calling this, the next `count(label)` will print 1 again.
If the label does not exist, this is a no-op.

# Examples

```tml
console::count("x")        // prints: x: 1
console::count("x")        // prints: x: 2
console::count_reset("x")
console::count("x")        // prints: x: 1
```
items.summary: Reset a named counter to 0.

items.name: group
items.doc:
Start a new indentation group.

Prints the label and increases the indentation level by one.
All subsequent output from `log`, `warn`, `error`, etc. will
be indented until `group_end` is called.

Groups can be nested up to 6 levels deep (visual indent caps
at 12 spaces).

# Examples

```tml
console::group("Processing items")
console::log("Item 1: OK")
console::log("Item 2: OK")
console::group_end()
```
items.summary: Start a new indentation group.

items.name: group_end
items.doc:
End the current indentation group.

Decreases the indentation level by one. If the indentation
is already at 0, this is a no-op.

# Examples

```tml
console::group("Section A")
console::log("inside group")
console::group_end()
console::log("back to normal")
```
items.summary: End the current indentation group.

items.name: assert
items.doc:
Assert a condition, printing a failure message if false.

If `condition` is `true`, does nothing. If `condition` is `false`,
prints `"Assertion failed: <message>"` to stdout.

This does NOT abort the program — it is a diagnostic tool for
development, not a hard assertion. For hard assertions that
panic, use `core::assert`.

# Examples

```tml
console::assert(x > 0, "x must be positive")
console::assert(list.len() < 100, "list too large")
```
items.summary: Assert a condition, printing a failure message if false.

items.name: table
items.summary: Print a list of strings in a simple table format.

modules.name: cipher
modules.doc:
Symmetric encryption and decryption.

This module provides symmetric cipher operations for encrypting and
decrypting data using secret keys.

# Supported Algorithms

| Algorithm | Key Size | Block/Nonce | Mode | Notes |
|-----------|----------|-------------|------|-------|
| AES-128-CBC | 128 bits | 128-bit IV | CBC | Requires padding |
| AES-192-CBC | 192 bits | 128-bit IV | CBC | Requires padding |
| AES-256-CBC | 256 bits | 128-bit IV | CBC | Requires padding |
| AES-128-CTR | 128 bits | 128-bit IV | CTR | Stream mode |
| AES-192-CTR | 192 bits | 128-bit IV | CTR | Stream mode |
| AES-256-CTR | 256 bits | 128-bit IV | CTR | Stream mode |
| AES-128-GCM | 128 bits | 96-bit nonce | GCM | AEAD, authenticated |
| AES-192-GCM | 192 bits | 96-bit nonce | GCM | AEAD, authenticated |
| AES-256-GCM | 256 bits | 96-bit nonce | GCM | AEAD, authenticated |
| AES-128-CCM | 128 bits | 56-104 bit | CCM | AEAD |
| AES-256-CCM | 256 bits | 56-104 bit | CCM | AEAD |
| ChaCha20-Poly1305 | 256 bits | 96-bit nonce | AEAD | Recommended |
| XChaCha20-Poly1305 | 256 bits | 192-bit nonce | AEAD | Extended nonce |

# AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data)

AEAD modes (GCM, CCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) provide both confidentiality and
authenticity. They produce an authentication tag that must be verified
during decryption.

# Examples

## AES-256-GCM Encryption (Recommended)

```tml
use std::crypto::{aes_gcm_encrypt, aes_gcm_decrypt, random_bytes}

let key = random_bytes(32)    // 256-bit key
let nonce = random_bytes(12)  // 96-bit nonce
let plaintext = "secret message"
let aad = "associated data"   // optional

// Encrypt
let (ciphertext, tag) = aes_gcm_encrypt(key, nonce, plaintext, aad)?

// Decrypt
let decrypted = aes_gcm_decrypt(key, nonce, ciphertext, aad, tag)?
```

## ChaCha20-Poly1305 (Alternative)

```tml
use std::crypto::{chacha20_poly1305_encrypt, chacha20_poly1305_decrypt, random_bytes}

let key = random_bytes(32)
let nonce = random_bytes(12)

let (ciphertext, tag) = chacha20_poly1305_encrypt(key, nonce, "message", "")?
let plaintext = chacha20_poly1305_decrypt(key, nonce, ciphertext, "", tag)?
```

## Streaming Encryption

```tml
use std::crypto::{Cipher, CipherAlgorithm, random_bytes}

let key = random_bytes(32)
let iv = random_bytes(16)

let cipher = Cipher::new(CipherAlgorithm::Aes256Cbc, key, iv)?
cipher.update("first chunk ")
cipher.update("second chunk")
let encrypted = cipher.finalize()?
```

modules.name: dh
modules.doc:
Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

This module provides classic Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange for
establishing shared secrets over insecure channels.

# Security Note

For new applications, prefer ECDH (elliptic curve DH) over classic DH
due to smaller key sizes and faster operations with equivalent security.

# Named Groups

| Group | Size | Security Level |
|-------|------|----------------|
| modp1 | 768 bits | Weak (deprecated) |
| modp2 | 1024 bits | Weak (deprecated) |
| modp5 | 1536 bits | Low |
| modp14 | 2048 bits | Medium |
| modp15 | 3072 bits | High |
| modp16 | 4096 bits | High |
| modp17 | 6144 bits | Very High |
| modp18 | 8192 bits | Very High |

# Examples

## Key Exchange with Named Group

```tml
use std::crypto::{create_dh_group, DhGroup}

// Alice
let alice = create_dh_group(DhGroup::Modp14)?
let alice_public = alice.public_key()

// Bob
let bob = create_dh_group(DhGroup::Modp14)?
let bob_public = bob.public_key()

// Compute shared secrets
let alice_secret = alice.compute_secret(bob_public)?
let bob_secret = bob.compute_secret(alice_public)?

// alice_secret == bob_secret
```

## Custom DH Parameters

```tml
use std::crypto::{create_dh, DiffieHellman}

// Create DH with custom prime and generator
let dh = create_dh(prime_bytes, generator_bytes)?
dh.generate_keys()

let shared_secret = dh.compute_secret(other_public_key)?
```

modules.name: ecdh
modules.doc:
Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key exchange.

ECDH provides the same security as classic DH with much smaller key sizes,
making it faster and more efficient.

# Supported Curves

| Curve | Size | Security Level | Notes |
|-------|------|----------------|-------|
| prime256v1 (P-256) | 256 bits | 128-bit | NIST, widely used |
| secp384r1 (P-384) | 384 bits | 192-bit | NIST |
| secp521r1 (P-521) | 521 bits | 256-bit | NIST |
| secp256k1 | 256 bits | 128-bit | Bitcoin/Ethereum |
| X25519 | 256 bits | 128-bit | Modern, recommended |
| X448 | 448 bits | 224-bit | Higher security |

# Recommendations

- For general use: **X25519** (fastest, constant-time)
- For higher security: **X448** or **P-384**
- For compatibility: **P-256** (widest support)
- For blockchain: **secp256k1**

# Examples

## X25519 Key Exchange (Recommended)

```tml
use std::crypto::{create_ecdh, EcCurve}

// Alice
let alice = create_ecdh(EcCurve::X25519)?
alice.generate_keys()
let alice_public = alice.public_key()

// Bob
let bob = create_ecdh(EcCurve::X25519)?
bob.generate_keys()
let bob_public = bob.public_key()

// Compute shared secrets
let alice_secret = alice.compute_secret(bob_public)?
let bob_secret = bob.compute_secret(alice_public)?

// alice_secret == bob_secret
```

## NIST P-256 Key Exchange

```tml
use std::crypto::{create_ecdh, EcCurve}

let ecdh = create_ecdh(EcCurve::P256)?
ecdh.generate_keys()

let public_key = ecdh.public_key()  // Send to peer
let shared_secret = ecdh.compute_secret(peer_public_key)?
```

## Derive Encryption Key from Shared Secret

```tml
use std::crypto::{create_ecdh, EcCurve, hkdf, HashAlgorithm}

let ecdh = create_ecdh(EcCurve::X25519)?
ecdh.generate_keys()

let shared_secret = ecdh.compute_secret(peer_public_key)?

// Derive encryption key using HKDF
let salt = random_bytes(32)
let key = hkdf(HashAlgorithm::Sha256, shared_secret, salt, "encryption", 32)?
```

modules.name: hash
modules.doc:
Cryptographic hash functions.

This module provides cryptographic hash functions for computing message digests.

# Supported Algorithms

| Algorithm | Output Size | Security | Notes |
|-----------|-------------|----------|-------|
| MD5 | 128 bits | Broken | Legacy only, do not use for security |
| SHA-1 | 160 bits | Weak | Deprecated, avoid for new applications |
| SHA-256 | 256 bits | Strong | Recommended for general use |
| SHA-384 | 384 bits | Strong | Higher security margin |
| SHA-512 | 512 bits | Strong | Best for 64-bit platforms |
| SHA-512/256 | 256 bits | Strong | SHA-512 truncated to 256 bits |

# Examples

## One-shot Hashing

```tml
use std::crypto::{sha256, sha512}

let hash1 = sha256("hello world")
let hash2 = sha512("hello world")

print("SHA-256: {hash1.to_hex()}\n")
print("SHA-512: {hash2.to_hex()}\n")
```

## Streaming Hash

```tml
use std::crypto::{Hash, HashAlgorithm}

let hash = Hash::create(HashAlgorithm::Sha256)
hash.update("hello ")
hash.update("world")
let digest = hash.digest()

print("Digest: {digest.to_hex()}\n")
```

modules.name: hmac
modules.doc:
HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code).

HMAC provides message authentication using a secret key combined with a
cryptographic hash function. It verifies both data integrity and authenticity.

# Supported Algorithms

| Algorithm | Output Size | Notes |
|-----------|-------------|-------|
| HMAC-MD5 | 128 bits | Legacy only, not secure |
| HMAC-SHA1 | 160 bits | Deprecated |
| HMAC-SHA256 | 256 bits | Recommended |
| HMAC-SHA384 | 384 bits | Higher security |
| HMAC-SHA512 | 512 bits | Best for 64-bit platforms |

# Examples

## One-shot HMAC

```tml
use std::crypto::hmac::{hmac_sha256}

let mut mac: HmacDigest = hmac_sha256("secret-key", "message")
print("HMAC: {mac.to_hex()}\n")
mac.destroy()
```

modules.name: kdf
modules.doc:
Key Derivation Functions.

This module provides key derivation functions for deriving cryptographic
keys from passwords, shared secrets, or other key material.

# Password Hashing

For password hashing, derive a key using:
1. **Argon2** (recommended) - Memory-hard, GPU-resistant (OpenSSL 3.2+)
2. **scrypt** - Memory-hard, widely supported
3. **PBKDF2** - CPU-intensive, FIPS compliant

# Key Derivation

For deriving keys from shared secrets (e.g., ECDH):
- **HKDF** - Extract-then-expand based on HMAC

# Security Recommendations

| Use Case | Recommended KDF | Parameters |
|----------|-----------------|------------|
| Password storage | Argon2id | m=65536, t=3, p=4 |
| Password-based encryption | Argon2id or scrypt | High memory |
| Key derivation from DH | HKDF-SHA256 | - |
| FIPS compliance | PBKDF2-SHA256 | 600,000+ iterations |

# Examples

## Argon2 Password Hashing

```tml
use std::crypto::{argon2, Argon2Variant, Argon2Params, random_bytes}

let params = Argon2Params::default()
let salt = random_bytes(16)
let hash = argon2(Argon2Variant::Argon2id, "password", salt, params)?
```

## scrypt Key Derivation

```tml
use std::crypto::{scrypt, ScryptParams, random_bytes}

let params = ScryptParams::default()
let salt = random_bytes(16)
let key = scrypt("password", salt, 32, params)?
```

## PBKDF2

```tml
use std::crypto::{pbkdf2, HashAlgorithm, random_bytes}

let salt = random_bytes(16)
let key = pbkdf2("password", salt, 100000, 32, HashAlgorithm::Sha256)?
```

## HKDF

```tml
use std::crypto::{hkdf, HashAlgorithm}

let ikm = shared_secret  // e.g., from ECDH
let salt = random_bytes(32)
let info = "encryption key"
let key = hkdf(HashAlgorithm::Sha256, ikm, salt, info, 32)?
```

items.name: argon2
items.signature: func argon2(variant: Argon2Variant, password: Str, salt: ref Buffer, key_length: I64, params: ref Argon2Params) -> CryptoResult[Buffer]
items.doc:
Derives a key using Argon2.

Argon2 is a modern password hashing algorithm that won the Password
Hashing Competition. It is designed to be memory-hard and resist
GPU cracking attacks.

# Parameters

- `variant`: Argon2 variant (Argon2id recommended)
- `password`: The password to hash
- `salt`: Random salt (at least 16 bytes)
- `key_length`: Desired output length in bytes
- `params`: Argon2 parameters

# Example

```tml
let params = Argon2Params::default()
let salt = random_bytes(16)
let hash = argon2(Argon2Variant::Argon2id, "password", salt, 32, params)?
```
items.summary: Derives a key using Argon2.

modules.name: key
modules.doc:
Cryptographic key management.

This module provides types and functions for working with cryptographic keys,
including symmetric (secret) keys and asymmetric (public/private) key pairs.

# Key Types

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`SecretKey`] | Symmetric key for encryption/HMAC |
| [`PrivateKey`] | Asymmetric private key for signing/decryption |
| [`PublicKey`] | Asymmetric public key for verification/encryption |
| [`KeyPair`] | Public and private key pair |

# Supported Key Algorithms

| Algorithm | Description | Typical Uses |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|
| RSA | RSA (2048-4096 bits) | Signatures, encryption |
| EC P-256 | NIST P-256 curve | ECDSA, ECDH |
| EC P-384 | NIST P-384 curve | ECDSA, ECDH |
| EC P-521 | NIST P-521 curve | ECDSA, ECDH |
| Ed25519 | Edwards curve | Signatures |
| Ed448 | Edwards curve | Signatures |
| X25519 | Curve25519 | Key exchange |
| X448 | Curve448 | Key exchange |
| DSA | Digital Signature Algorithm | Signatures (legacy) |
| DH | Diffie-Hellman | Key exchange |

# Examples

## Generate RSA Key Pair

```tml
use std::crypto::{generate_key_pair, KeyType}

let keypair = generate_key_pair(KeyType::Rsa, 2048)?
let public_pem = keypair.public_key.to_pem()
let private_pem = keypair.private_key.to_pem()
```

## Generate Ed25519 Key Pair

```tml
use std::crypto::{generate_key_pair, KeyType}

let keypair = generate_key_pair(KeyType::Ed25519, 0)?
```

## Generate Symmetric Key

```tml
use std::crypto::{generate_key, SecretKey}

let key = generate_key(32)?  // 256-bit key
```

## Import/Export Keys

```tml
use std::crypto::{create_private_key, create_public_key, KeyFormat}

// From PEM
let private_key = create_private_key(pem_string, KeyFormat::Pem)?

// Export to DER
let der_bytes = private_key.to_der()
```

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
Cryptographic primitives and utilities.

This module provides comprehensive cryptographic functionality including:

- **Hash functions**: SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3, MD5, BLAKE2, BLAKE3
- **HMAC**: Keyed-hash message authentication codes
- **Ciphers**: AES, ChaCha20-Poly1305 symmetric encryption
- **Signatures**: RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519, Ed448 digital signatures
- **Key generation**: Symmetric and asymmetric key generation
- **Key derivation**: PBKDF2, scrypt, HKDF, Argon2
- **Random**: Cryptographically secure random number generation
- **X.509**: Certificate parsing and verification
- **Diffie-Hellman**: DH and ECDH key exchange
- **RSA**: Public-key encryption/decryption

# Hash Functions

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`Hash`] | Streaming hash computation |
| [`Hasher`] | Behavior for hashable types |
| [`sha1()`] | Compute SHA-1 hash (160-bit) |
| [`sha256()`] | Compute SHA-256 hash (256-bit) |
| [`sha384()`] | Compute SHA-384 hash (384-bit) |
| [`sha512()`] | Compute SHA-512 hash (512-bit) |
| [`sha3_256()`] | Compute SHA3-256 hash (256-bit) |
| [`sha3_384()`] | Compute SHA3-384 hash (384-bit) |
| [`sha3_512()`] | Compute SHA3-512 hash (512-bit) |
| [`md5()`] | Compute MD5 hash (128-bit, legacy) |
| [`blake2b()`] | Compute BLAKE2b hash (up to 512-bit) |
| [`blake2s()`] | Compute BLAKE2s hash (up to 256-bit) |
| [`blake3()`] | Compute BLAKE3 hash (256-bit) |

# HMAC

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`Hmac`] | HMAC computation object |
| [`hmac_sha256()`] | Compute HMAC-SHA256 |
| [`hmac_sha512()`] | Compute HMAC-SHA512 |

# Symmetric Encryption

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`Cipher`] | Encryption object |
| [`Decipher`] | Decryption object |
| [`CipherAlgorithm`] | Supported cipher algorithms |
| [`aes_encrypt()`] | AES encryption helper |
| [`aes_decrypt()`] | AES decryption helper |

# Digital Signatures

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`Signer`] | Signature creation object |
| [`Verifier`] | Signature verification object |
| [`sign()`] | Sign data with private key |
| [`verify()`] | Verify signature with public key |

# Key Management

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`SecretKey`] | Symmetric key object |
| [`PrivateKey`] | Asymmetric private key |
| [`PublicKey`] | Asymmetric public key |
| [`KeyPair`] | Public/private key pair |
| [`generate_key()`] | Generate symmetric key |
| [`generate_key_pair()`] | Generate asymmetric key pair |

# Key Derivation

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`pbkdf2()`] | PBKDF2 key derivation |
| [`scrypt()`] | scrypt key derivation |
| [`hkdf()`] | HKDF key derivation |
| [`argon2()`] | Argon2 password hashing |

# Random Number Generation

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`random_bytes()`] | Generate random bytes |
| [`random_int()`] | Generate random integer |
| [`random_uuid()`] | Generate random UUID v4 |
| [`SecureRandom`] | CSPRNG instance |

# Certificates

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`X509Certificate`] | X.509 certificate |
| [`X509Chain`] | Certificate chain |

# Key Exchange

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`DiffieHellman`] | Classic DH key exchange |
| [`Ecdh`] | Elliptic curve DH |

# Examples

## Hashing

```tml
use std::crypto::{sha256, Hash, HashAlgorithm}

// One-shot hashing
let digest = sha256("hello world")
print(digest.to_hex())

// Streaming hash
let hash = Hash::new(HashAlgorithm::Sha256)
hash.update("hello ")
hash.update("world")
let result = hash.digest()
```

## HMAC

```tml
use std::crypto::{Hmac, HashAlgorithm}

let hmac = Hmac::new(HashAlgorithm::Sha256, "secret-key")
hmac.update("message to authenticate")
let mac = hmac.digest()
```

## Encryption

```tml
use std::crypto::{Cipher, CipherAlgorithm, random_bytes}

let key = random_bytes(32)  // 256-bit key
let iv = random_bytes(16)   // 128-bit IV

let cipher = Cipher::new(CipherAlgorithm::Aes256Cbc, key, iv)
cipher.update("secret message")
let encrypted = cipher.finalize()
```

## Key Generation

```tml
use std::crypto::{generate_key_pair, KeyType}

let keypair = generate_key_pair(KeyType::Rsa, 2048)
let public_pem = keypair.public_key.to_pem()
let private_pem = keypair.private_key.to_pem()
```

## Password Hashing

```tml
use std::crypto::{argon2, Argon2Variant}

let hash = argon2(
    Argon2Variant::Argon2id,
    "user-password",
    random_bytes(16),  // salt
    3,                 // iterations
    65536,             // memory (KB)
    4,                 // parallelism
    32,                // output length
)
```

modules.name: rsa
modules.doc:
RSA encryption and decryption.

This module provides RSA public-key encryption and decryption operations.

# Security Notes

- For signing/verification, use the `sign` module instead
- RSA encryption should only be used for small data (e.g., symmetric keys)
- For encrypting larger data, use hybrid encryption (RSA + AES)
- Minimum recommended key size: 2048 bits
- Prefer OAEP padding over PKCS#1 v1.5

# Padding Schemes

| Padding | Use Case | Notes |
|---------|----------|-------|
| OAEP | General encryption | Recommended |
| PKCS#1 v1.5 | Legacy compatibility | Avoid if possible |
| No padding | Raw RSA | Dangerous, avoid |

# Maximum Data Size

The maximum data size that can be encrypted depends on the key size
and padding scheme:

- OAEP with SHA-256: key_bytes - 66
- PKCS#1 v1.5: key_bytes - 11
- No padding: key_bytes

For a 2048-bit key (256 bytes): max 190 bytes with OAEP/SHA-256.

# Examples

## Encrypt with Public Key

```tml
use std::crypto::{public_encrypt, RsaPadding, PublicKey}

let encrypted = public_encrypt(public_key, data, RsaPadding::OaepSha256)?
```

## Decrypt with Private Key

```tml
use std::crypto::{private_decrypt, RsaPadding, PrivateKey}

let decrypted = private_decrypt(private_key, encrypted, RsaPadding::OaepSha256)?
```

## Hybrid Encryption (RSA + AES)

```tml
use std::crypto::{
    public_encrypt, private_decrypt, RsaPadding,
    aes_gcm_encrypt, aes_gcm_decrypt,
    random_bytes,
}

// Encrypt
func hybrid_encrypt(public_key: ref PublicKey, data: ref Buffer) -> (Buffer, Buffer) {
    let aes_key = random_bytes(32)
    let nonce = random_bytes(12)

    // Encrypt the AES key with RSA
    let encrypted_key = public_encrypt(public_key, ref aes_key, RsaPadding::OaepSha256)?

    // Encrypt the data with AES
    let (ciphertext, tag) = aes_gcm_encrypt(aes_key, nonce, data, Buffer::empty())?

    // Combine nonce + ciphertext + tag
    let encrypted_data = concat(nonce, ciphertext, tag)

    return (encrypted_key, encrypted_data)
}
```

modules.name: sign
modules.doc:
Digital signatures.

This module provides digital signature creation and verification using
asymmetric cryptography.

# Supported Algorithms

| Algorithm | Key Type | Description |
|-----------|----------|-------------|
| RSA-SHA256 | RSA | RSA with SHA-256 |
| RSA-SHA384 | RSA | RSA with SHA-384 |
| RSA-SHA512 | RSA | RSA with SHA-512 |
| RSA-PSS | RSA | RSA-PSS (probabilistic) |
| ECDSA-SHA256 | EC P-256 | ECDSA with SHA-256 |
| ECDSA-SHA384 | EC P-384 | ECDSA with SHA-384 |
| ECDSA-SHA512 | EC P-521 | ECDSA with SHA-512 |
| Ed25519 | Ed25519 | EdDSA with Curve25519 |
| Ed448 | Ed448 | EdDSA with Curve448 |

# Examples

## One-shot Signing

```tml
use std::crypto::{sign, verify, generate_key_pair, KeyType}

let keypair = generate_key_pair(KeyType::Ed25519)?
let message = "data to sign"

// Sign
let signature = sign(SignatureAlgorithm::Ed25519, keypair.private_key, message)?

// Verify
let valid = verify(SignatureAlgorithm::Ed25519, keypair.public_key, message, signature)?
assert(valid)
```

## Streaming Signing

```tml
use std::crypto::{Signer, SignatureAlgorithm, PrivateKey}

let signer = Signer::new(SignatureAlgorithm::RsaSha256, private_key)?
signer.update("first part of message")
signer.update("second part")
let signature = signer.sign()?
```

## Streaming Verification

```tml
use std::crypto::{Verifier, SignatureAlgorithm, PublicKey}

let verifier = Verifier::new(SignatureAlgorithm::RsaSha256, public_key)?
verifier.update("first part of message")
verifier.update("second part")
let valid = verifier.verify(signature)?
```

This module provides functionality for parsing, validating, and working
with X.509 certificates, which are the standard format for public key
certificates used in TLS/SSL.

- Verify certificate signatures
- Check validity period
- Validate hostname/IP/email
- Certificate chain verification
- Access certificate fields (subject, issuer, extensions)

modules.name: reference
modules.doc:
Cross-language benchmark reference.

Equivalent benchmark implementations for comparison:

## Rust (SQLx)
```rust
use sqlx::sqlite::SqlitePoolOptions;
let pool = SqlitePoolOptions::new().connect(":memory:").await?;
sqlx::query("INSERT INTO World (id, randomNumber) VALUES (?, ?)")
    .bind(1).bind(42).execute(&pool).await?;
```

## Go (database/sql)
```go
db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite3", ":memory:")
db.Exec("INSERT INTO World (id, randomNumber) VALUES (?, ?)", 1, 42)
```

## Node.js (better-sqlite3)
```javascript
const db = new Database(':memory:');
db.prepare('INSERT INTO World (id, randomNumber) VALUES (?, ?)').run(1, 42);
```

## TML (std::db)
```tml
let conn = SqliteConnection::open_in_memory()!
conn.execute("INSERT INTO World (id, randomNumber) VALUES (1, 42)")!
```

modules.name: template
modules.doc:
Template for creating a new TML database driver.

## Steps to create a new driver (e.g., PostgreSQL):

### Step 1: Create module directory
```
lib/std/src/db/postgres/
  mod.tml         — module exports
  connection.tml  — PgConnection, impl Connection
  statement.tml   — PgStatement, impl PreparedStatement
  dialect.tml     — PgDialect, impl Dialect
  types.tml       — PostgreSQL ↔ ColumnType mapping
```

### Step 2: Implement Connection behavior
```tml
use std::db::driver::connection::Connection
use std::db::error::{DbError, DbErrorKind}

pub type PgConnection { handle: I64 }

impl Connection for PgConnection {
    pub func execute(this, sql: Str) -> Outcome[I64, DbError] { ... }
    pub func is_alive(this) -> Bool { ... }
    pub func close(mut this) { ... }
}
```

### Step 3: Guard with feature flag
In `db/mod.tml`:
```tml
#ifdef DB_POSTGRES
pub mod postgres
#endif
```

### Step 4: Update features.tml
Add `has_postgres()` function.
modules.summary: Template for creating a new TML database driver.

Inspired by TypeORM's eager relations feature and `QueryBuilder::leftJoinAndSelect`.

Generates a SELECT query with LEFT JOINs for all given relations.

Produces:
```sql
SELECT * FROM <table>
  LEFT JOIN <r1.foreign_table> ON <table>.<r1.local_key> = <r1.foreign_table>.<r1.foreign_key>
  LEFT JOIN <r2.foreign_table> ON …
```

items.signature: func load_with[C](conn: ref C, table: Str, pk: I64, relations: ref List[Relation]) -> Outcome[Str, DbError] where C: Connection

Binds `pk` as a WHERE condition (`<table>.id = <pk>`) on top of the JOIN query,
executes it, and returns the SQL string that was run.

Returns `Ok(sql)` on success, `Err(e)` if execution fails.

modules.name: entity
modules.doc:
Entity definition — the core of the ORM.

# TypeORM-Style Entity Definition

Use field-level decorators to declare database entities:

```tml
@entity("users")
type User {
    @primary_column
    id: I64,

    @column
    name: Str,

    @column @nullable
    age: I64,

    @column
    email: Str
}
```

Then register the entity metadata at runtime:

```tml
let users = EntityMeta::new("users", "id")
    .column(Column::primary("id"))
    .column(Column::text("name"))
    .column(Column::integer("age").set_nullable())
    .column(Column::text("email"))

sync_entity(conn, ref users)  // CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (...)
```

The `@entity`, `@column`, `@primary_column`, and `@nullable` decorators
are parsed by the compiler and stored in the AST. They serve as the
canonical way to declare which types are database entities.
modules.summary: Entity definition — the core of the ORM.

`having`, `with_relation`, and `count_sql`.

Multiple calls to `filter` are ANDed together automatically,
mimicking Django/TypeORM's chainable query builder pattern.

items.name: Expr
items.doc:
A SQL expression that can be rendered to a SQL string.

Uses a flat struct with an integer tag instead of a recursive enum
to avoid nested-generic codegen issues in the current compiler.

Tag values:
  0 = Column reference (`text` holds the column name)
  1 = Integer literal  (`int_val` holds the value)
  2 = Float literal    (`float_val` holds the value)
  3 = String literal   (`text` holds the value)
  4 = NULL literal
  5 = Comparison       (`op` 0-6, `left_sql`/`right_sql` pre-rendered)
  6 = Logic (AND/OR)   (`op` 0=AND 1=OR, `left_sql`/`right_sql` pre-rendered)
  8 = IS NULL          (`left_sql` pre-rendered)
  9 = IS NOT NULL      (`left_sql` pre-rendered)
 10 = Raw SQL          (`text` holds the raw fragment)
 11 = Positional param (`int_val` holds the 1-based index, renders as `?`)
 12 = Named param      (`text` holds the name, renders as `:name`)
 13 = IN subquery      (`left_sql` holds col name, `right_sql` holds SELECT SQL)
items.summary: A SQL expression that can be rendered to a SQL string.

This module bridges `std::sqlite` with the `std::db` driver behaviors,

Maps a SQLite declared type string (e.g. "INTEGER", "VARCHAR(255)")
to a ColumnType.

Uses prefix matching to handle SQLite's type affinity rules:
- "INT" prefix → Integer
- "REAL", "FLOAT", "DOUBLE" → Float
- "BLOB" → Blob
- "BOOL" → Boolean
- "TIME", "DATE" → Timestamp
- Everything else → Text

| Variant     | Meaning                                      |
|-------------|----------------------------------------------|
| Null        | SQL NULL                                     |
| Bool(v)     | Boolean true/false                           |
| Integer(v)  | 64-bit signed integer                        |
| Float(v)    | 64-bit IEEE 754 float                        |
| Text(v)     | UTF-8 string                                 |

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
Event-driven programming primitives.

This module provides an `EventEmitter` type for publish/subscribe
patterns, inspired by Node.js's `events` module.

# Core Type

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`EventEmitter`] | Named-event dispatcher with ordered listeners |

Listeners are `func(I64)` function pointers passed as I64.

# Features

- **on** — Register a listener
- **once** — Register a one-time listener
- **off** — Remove a listener
- **emit** — Synchronously call all listeners
- **emit_async** — Defer listeners to EventLoop pending queue
- **emit_next_tick** — Defer listeners to EventLoop next-tick queue
- **prepend_listener** — Register listener to be called first
- **listeners_of** — Get all listeners for an event
- **event_names** — Get all registered event names

# Example

```tml
use std::events::EventEmitter

func on_click(data: I64) {
    print("clicked!\n")
}

var emitter = EventEmitter::new()
emitter.on("click", on_click as I64)
emitter.emit("click", 0)
emitter.destroy()
```

modules.name: observable
modules.doc:
Reactive programming primitives — Observable[T] and Subject types.

Implements the Observer pattern with push-based value streams, inspired
by RxJS. Values are pushed from producers to consumers through callbacks.

# Working Types

- **`ObservableI32`** — Lazy push-based value stream with enum-based sources.
  Supports factory functions (of2, of3, from_list, empty, never, throw) and
  operators (map, filter, take, skip, scan, distinct, merge, concat).

- **Subject state functions** — `subject_new_i32()` returns a `List[I64]`
  tracking completed/error/next_id state. Observer callbacks must be
  managed by the caller due to function-pointer-in-List codegen limitations.

# Known Limitations (codegen bugs)

- Cross-module closures: closure symbols not emitted in LLVM IR
- Struct GEP: structs with List fields crash when passed by value
- List[func(T)]: function pointer stride/layout causes runtime crash
- These prevent a fully-encapsulated Subject type. The workaround is
  state-only subjects with caller-managed callbacks.

modules.name: promise
modules.doc:
JavaScript-style Promise[T] for asynchronous value resolution.

A `Promise[T]` represents a value that will be available at some point
in the future. Unlike futures (which are poll-based), promises use a
callback/resolution model inspired by JavaScript's `Promise`.

# State Machine

A promise is always in one of three states:

- **Pending** — The value is not yet available
- **Fulfilled(T)** — The operation completed successfully with a value
- **Rejected(Str)** — The operation failed with an error message

Once a promise transitions from Pending to Fulfilled or Rejected,
its state never changes again.

# Creating Promises

```tml
use std::promise::Promise

// Immediately resolved
let p: Promise[I32] = Promise::resolve(42)
assert(p.is_fulfilled())

// Immediately rejected
let p: Promise[I32] = Promise::reject("failed")
assert(p.is_rejected())
```

# Chaining

```tml
let doubled: Promise[I32] = promise_map_i32(Promise::resolve(21), do(x: I32) -> I32 { x * 2 })
// doubled is fulfilled with 42
```

# Combinators

- `promise_all_i32(promises)` — Resolves when ALL promises resolve
- `promise_race_i32(promises)` — Settles with whichever settles first
- `promise_any_i32(promises)` — Resolves with first fulfillment
- `promise_all_settled_i32(promises)` — Always resolves with all states
modules.summary: JavaScript-style Promise[T] for asynchronous value resolution.

- `Fulfilled(T)` — The operation succeeded with the contained value
- `Rejected(Str)` — The operation failed with an error message

A JavaScript-style promise for asynchronous value resolution.

`Promise[T]` wraps a `PromiseState[T]` behind a `Shared` reference-counted
pointer, allowing multiple consumers to observe the same promise's outcome.

Promises are eagerly resolved — they do not require polling. Once created
in a `Fulfilled` or `Rejected` state, the value is immediately available.

# Thread Safety

`Promise[T]` uses `Shared[T]` (non-atomic reference counting) and is
**not thread-safe**. This matches JavaScript's single-threaded Promise
semantics. For thread-safe async, use `Future` with an executor instead.

# Examples

```tml
use std::promise::Promise

let p: Promise[I32] = Promise::resolve(42)
assert(p.is_fulfilled())
assert_eq(p.value(), Just(42))

let failed: Promise[I32] = Promise::reject("timeout")
assert(failed.is_rejected())
assert_eq(failed.error(), Just("timeout"))
```
items.summary: A JavaScript-style promise for asynchronous value resolution.

items.name: promise_map_i32
items.signature: func promise_map_i32(p: Promise[I32], f: func(I32) -> I32) -> Promise[I32]
items.doc:
Maps a fulfilled I32 promise through a transformation function.

If the source promise is fulfilled, applies `f` to the value and wraps the
result in a new fulfilled promise. If the source is rejected, propagates
the rejection. If pending, propagates pending.

# Examples

```tml
let p: Promise[I32] = Promise::resolve(21)
let doubled: Promise[I32] = promise_map_i32(p, do(x: I32) -> I32 { x * 2 })
assert_eq(doubled.unwrap(), 42)
```
items.summary: Maps a fulfilled I32 promise through a transformation function.

items.name: promise_catch_i32
items.signature: func promise_catch_i32(p: Promise[I32], f: func(Str) -> I32) -> Promise[I32]
items.doc:
Handles rejection of an I32 promise with a recovery function.

If the promise is rejected, applies `f` to the error message to produce
a recovery value. If fulfilled, passes through unchanged.

# Examples

```tml
let failed: Promise[I32] = Promise::reject("oops")
let recovered: Promise[I32] = promise_catch_i32(failed, do(e: Str) -> I32 { -1 })
assert_eq(recovered.unwrap(), -1)
```
items.summary: Handles rejection of an I32 promise with a recovery function.

items.name: promise_finally_i32
items.signature: func promise_finally_i32(p: Promise[I32], cleanup: func()) -> Promise[I32]
items.doc:
Runs a cleanup function regardless of the promise state.

The cleanup function receives no arguments and its return value is ignored.
The original promise state is propagated unchanged.
items.summary: Runs a cleanup function regardless of the promise state.

items.name: promise_all_i32
items.doc:
Waits for all promises to fulfill, or rejects on the first rejection.

Given a list of I32 promises, returns a new promise that:
- Fulfills with a `List[I32]` of all values (in order) if ALL fulfill
- Rejects with the first rejection reason if ANY rejects
- Remains pending if any promise is still pending and none rejected

# Examples

```tml
var promises: List[Promise[I32]] = List::new(4)
promises.push(Promise::resolve(1))
promises.push(Promise::resolve(2))
promises.push(Promise::resolve(3))
let all: Promise[List[I32]] = promise_all_i32(promises)
assert(all.is_fulfilled())
```
items.summary: Waits for all promises to fulfill, or rejects on the first rejection.

items.name: promise_race_i32
items.doc:
Returns the first settled promise (fulfilled or rejected).

Given a list of I32 promises, returns a new promise that settles with
the same state as whichever input promise settled first (by index order).

# Examples

```tml
var promises: List[Promise[I32]] = List::new(4)
promises.push(Promise::pending())
promises.push(Promise::resolve(42))
let winner: Promise[I32] = promise_race_i32(promises)
assert_eq(winner.unwrap(), 42)
```
items.summary: Returns the first settled promise (fulfilled or rejected).

items.name: promise_any_i32
items.doc:
Returns the first fulfilled promise, or rejects if all reject.

Given a list of I32 promises, returns a new promise that:
- Fulfills with the first fulfilled value
- Rejects with "All promises rejected" if ALL reject
- Remains pending if any is pending and none fulfilled
items.summary: Returns the first fulfilled promise, or rejects if all reject.

items.name: promise_all_settled_i32
items.doc:
Returns the settlement state of all promises.

Always fulfills (never rejects). The result is a list of `PromiseState[I32]`
values, one per input promise. Each state is either `Fulfilled(v)` or
`Rejected(e)`. If any input is still pending, the result promise is pending.
items.summary: Returns the settlement state of all promises.

modules.name: exception
modules.doc:
Exception class hierarchy for error handling.

This module provides a C#-style exception hierarchy for structured error
handling in TML applications.

# Main Types

| Exception | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [`Exception`] | Base exception class |
| [`ArgumentException`] | Invalid argument provided |
| [`ArgumentNullException`] | Null argument when non-null expected |
| [`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`] | Argument outside valid range |
| [`InvalidOperationException`] | Operation invalid for current state |
| [`NotSupportedException`] | Operation not supported |
| [`NotImplementedException`] | Method not yet implemented |
| [`IndexOutOfRangeException`] | Index outside array bounds |
| [`KeyNotFoundException`] | Key not found in dictionary |
| [`IOException`] | I/O operation failure |
| [`FileNotFoundException`] | File does not exist |
| [`ArithmeticException`] | Arithmetic error (overflow, divide by zero) |
| [`FormatException`] | Invalid format string |
| [`InvalidCastException`] | Invalid type conversion |
| [`TimeoutException`] | Operation timed out |

# Example

```tml
use std::exception::*

func validate_age(age: I32) -> Outcome[I32, Exception] {
    if age < 0 {
        return Err(ArgumentOutOfRangeException::create("age", age, "Age cannot be negative"))
    }
    return Ok(age)
}
```
modules.summary: Exception class hierarchy for error handling.

modules.name: bufio
modules.doc:
Buffered I/O wrappers for `File`.

Provides [`BufReader`] and [`BufWriter`] to reduce the number of
underlying system calls by batching reads and writes in memory.
[`LineWriter`] is a convenience wrapper that flushes on every newline.

# Example

```tml
use std::file::{File, BufReader, BufWriter}

let br: BufReader = BufReader::open("data.txt")
let line: Str = br.read_line()
br.close()

let bw: BufWriter = BufWriter::open("out.txt")
bw.write("hello\n")
bw.close()   // flushes automatically
```

modules.name: glob
modules.doc:
High-performance glob pattern matching.

Find files and directories matching glob patterns with support for
wildcards, recursive descent, character classes, and alternation.

# Supported Patterns

| Pattern | Matches |
|---------|---------|
| `*` | Any characters within a single path segment |
| `?` | Exactly one character |
| `**` | Zero or more directories (recursive) |
| `[abc]` | Any character in the set |
| `[a-z]` | Any character in the range |
| `[!abc]` | Any character NOT in the set |
| `{a,b}` | Any of the alternatives |

# Examples

```tml
use std::glob::Glob

// Find all .tml files recursively
var g: Glob = Glob::find("src", "**/*.tml")
loop {
    let path: Str = g.next()
    if path == "" { break }
    print("{path}\n")
}
g.free()

// Simple pattern matching (no filesystem)
use std::glob::matches
assert(matches("*.tml", "main.tml"))
assert(not matches("*.tml", "main.rs"))
```

modules.name: hash
modules.doc:
Fast non-cryptographic hash functions.

This module provides fast hash functions suitable for checksums, ETags,
hash tables, and data fingerprinting. These are **NOT** cryptographically
secure and should not be used for passwords or security-sensitive hashing.

# Supported Algorithms

| Algorithm | Output Size | Speed | Use Case |
|-----------|-------------|-------|----------|
| FNV-1a (32-bit) | 32 bits | Very Fast | Short strings, hash tables |
| FNV-1a (64-bit) | 64 bits | Very Fast | General purpose, ETags |
| Murmur2 (32-bit) | 32 bits | Fast | Hash tables, checksums |
| Murmur2 (64-bit) | 64 bits | Fast | ETags, fingerprinting |

# Examples

## HTTP ETag Generation

```tml
use std::hash::{fnv1a64, murmur2_64}

let content = "Hello, World!"
let etag = fnv1a64(content).to_hex()
print("ETag: \"{etag}\"\n")

// With Murmur2 (seeded for uniqueness)
let etag2 = murmur2_64(content, 0).to_hex()
print("ETag: \"{etag2}\"\n")
```

## Content Checksums

```tml
use std::hash::fnv1a32

let data = "Some data to checksum"
let checksum = fnv1a32(data)
print("Checksum: {checksum.to_hex()}\n")
```

# Security Warning

These hash functions are designed for speed, not security:
- **Do NOT use for passwords** - use `std::crypto::kdf` instead
- **Do NOT use for signatures** - use `std::crypto::sign` instead
- **Do NOT use for MACs** - use `std::crypto::hmac` instead

For cryptographic hashing, use `std::crypto::hash` (SHA-256, SHA-512, etc.)

items.name: fnv1a32
items.doc:
Computes the FNV-1a 32-bit hash of a string.

FNV-1a (Fowler-Noll-Vo) is a fast, non-cryptographic hash function
with good distribution properties. The 32-bit variant is ideal for
hash tables and short strings.

# Examples

```tml
use std::hash::fnv1a32

let hash = fnv1a32("hello")
print("Hash: {hash.to_hex()}\n")
```

# Algorithm

```text
hash = FNV_OFFSET_BASIS (2166136261)
for each byte:
    hash = hash XOR byte
    hash = hash * FNV_PRIME (16777619)
return hash
```
items.summary: Computes the FNV-1a 32-bit hash of a string.

items.name: fnv1a32_bytes
items.doc:
Computes the FNV-1a 32-bit hash of binary data.

# Examples

```tml
use std::hash::fnv1a32_bytes
use std::collections::Buffer

let buf = Buffer::from_bytes([0x01, 0x02, 0x03])
let hash = fnv1a32_bytes(ref buf)
```
items.summary: Computes the FNV-1a 32-bit hash of binary data.

items.name: fnv1a64
items.doc:
Computes the FNV-1a 64-bit hash of a string.

The 64-bit variant provides better collision resistance and is
recommended for ETags, content fingerprinting, and general use.

# Examples

```tml
use std::hash::fnv1a64

// Generate an ETag for HTTP caching
let content = read_file("index.html")
let etag = fnv1a64(content).to_hex()
set_header("ETag", "\"{etag}\"")
```

# Algorithm

```text
hash = FNV_OFFSET_BASIS (14695981039346656037)
for each byte:
    hash = hash XOR byte
    hash = hash * FNV_PRIME (1099511628211)
return hash
```
items.summary: Computes the FNV-1a 64-bit hash of a string.

items.summary: Computes the FNV-1a 64-bit hash of binary data.

items.name: murmur2_32
items.signature: func murmur2_32(data: Str, seed: U32) -> Hash32
items.doc:
Computes the MurmurHash2 32-bit hash of a string.

MurmurHash2 was designed by Austin Appleby and provides excellent
distribution with good performance. It accepts a seed value for
varying hash sequences.

# Arguments

* `data` - The string to hash
* `seed` - A seed value (use 0 for default)

# Examples

```tml
use std::hash::murmur2_32

let hash1 = murmur2_32("hello", 0)
let hash2 = murmur2_32("hello", 42)  // Different seed, different hash
```
items.summary: Computes the MurmurHash2 32-bit hash of a string.

items.signature: func murmur2_64(data: Str, seed: U64) -> Hash64
items.doc:
Computes the MurmurHash2 64-bit hash of a string.

This is MurmurHash64A, optimized for 64-bit platforms. It provides
excellent distribution and is suitable for ETags and fingerprinting.

# Arguments

* `data` - The string to hash
* `seed` - A seed value (use 0 for default)

# Examples

```tml
use std::hash::murmur2_64

// Generate an ETag with a server-specific seed
let server_seed: U64 = 0xDEADBEEF
let etag = murmur2_64(content, server_seed).to_hex()
```

modules.name: controller
modules.summary: Controller pattern for organizing HTTP route handlers.

items.name: Controller
items.doc:
A behavior for types that group HTTP route handlers under a URL prefix.

Implementing `Controller` on a type allows it to register a set of
related routes with an `App`. Each controller typically handles one
domain (users, products, auth, etc.).

# Required Methods

- `prefix()` — The base URL path for this controller's routes
- `register()` — Registers all routes with the given `App`

# Conventions

- The prefix should start with `/` (e.g., `"/users"`, `"/api/v1/products"`)
- Route paths passed to `app.get()`, etc. should include the full prefix
- Handlers are passed as `I64` function pointers per the App API
items.summary: A behavior for types that group HTTP route handlers under a URL prefix.

methods.name: prefix
methods.doc:
Returns the URL prefix for this controller's routes.

This is used for documentation and introspection. The actual
route paths are registered in `register()`.

# Examples

```tml
func prefix(this) -> Str { return "/users" }
```
methods.summary: Returns the URL prefix for this controller's routes.

methods.name: register
methods.signature: func register(this, app: mut ref App)
methods.doc:
Registers all routes for this controller with the given application.

Implementations should call `app.get()`, `app.post()`, etc. to
register their handlers.

# Examples

```tml
func register(this, app: mut ref App) {
    app.get("/users", list_users as I64)
    app.post("/users", create_user as I64)
    app.get("/users/:id", get_user as I64)
    app.put("/users/:id", update_user as I64)
    app.delete("/users/:id", delete_user as I64)
}
```
methods.summary: Registers all routes for this controller with the given application.

items.name: ControllerFn
items.summary: A controller registration function.

items.name: register_controllers
items.signature: func register_controllers(app: mut ref App, controllers: List[func(mut ref App)])
items.doc:
Registers multiple controller registration functions with an App.

This is a convenience function for applying many controllers at once.
Each function in the list is called with a mutable reference to the App.

# Arguments

- `app` — The application to register routes on
- `controllers` — A list of controller registration functions

# Examples

```tml
var controllers: List[ControllerFn] = List::new(4)
controllers.push(register_user_routes)
controllers.push(register_product_routes)
controllers.push(register_auth_routes)

var app: App = App::new()
register_controllers(ref app, controllers)
app.listen(3000)
```
items.summary: Registers multiple controller registration functions with an App.

items.name: register_controller
items.signature: func register_controller(app: mut ref App, register_fn: func(mut ref App))
items.doc:
Registers a single controller registration function with an App.

This is a convenience wrapper for calling a registration function.

# Examples

```tml
var app: App = App::new()
register_controller(ref app, register_user_routes)
```
items.summary: Registers a single controller registration function with an App.

items.name: ControllerInfo
items.doc:
Metadata about a controller for introspection and documentation.

This type pairs a URL prefix with a registration function, allowing
applications to enumerate their controllers and their prefixes.

# Examples

```tml
let info = ControllerInfo::new("/users", register_user_routes)
println("Controller: " + info.prefix)
info.register(ref app)
```
items.summary: Metadata about a controller for introspection and documentation.

modules.name: connection
modules.doc:
HTTP/2 connection management (RFC 7540 Sections 3-6).

Manages the connection-level state: stream table, HPACK contexts,
settings negotiation, flow control, and GOAWAY handling.

# Design

The stream table is implemented as a flat array of stream pointers
(allocated via `mem_alloc`) indexed by a linear scan. This avoids
generic HashMap[I64, H2Stream] codegen issues. HTTP/2 connections
typically have < 100 concurrent streams, so linear scan is fine.

All "send" methods return a `Buffer` containing the encoded frame(s)
to write to the wire. The caller is responsible for actually sending.

items.name: H2Settings

H2Frame values and it will:

  - H2_CONN_EVENT_DATA: accumulate request body
  - H2_CONN_EVENT_GOAWAY: stop accepting new streams
  etc.

modules.name: frame
modules.doc:
HTTP/2 binary frame codec (RFC 7540).

Implements encoding and decoding of HTTP/2 frames with their 9-byte headers.
All multi-byte integers use network byte order (big-endian) per the spec.

# Frame Format

```
+-----------------------------------------------+
|                 Length (24 bits)               |
+---------------+---------------+---------------+
|   Type (8)    |   Flags (8)   |
+-+-------------+---------------+------+--------+
|R|                 Stream ID (31 bits)         |
+-+---------------------------------------------+
|                Frame Payload ...               |
+-----------------------------------------------+
```

# Example

```tml
use std::http::h2::frame::{H2Frame, H2FrameType, h2_encode_frame, h2_decode_frame}

let frame = H2Frame.new(H2FrameType::Ping, 0, 0, Buffer::new(8))
let encoded = h2_encode_frame(ref frame)
```

items.doc:
Encode an HTTP/2 frame header and payload into a Buffer.

The output buffer contains:
  - Bytes 0-2: payload length (24-bit big-endian)
  - Byte 3: frame type
  - Byte 4: flags
  - Bytes 5-8: stream identifier (31-bit big-endian, R bit = 0)
  - Bytes 9+: payload

Parameters are passed individually to avoid struct-by-value codegen issues.
items.summary: Encode an HTTP/2 frame header and payload into a Buffer.

modules.name: hpack
modules.doc:
HPACK header compression (RFC 7541).

Implements encoding and decoding of HTTP/2 headers using the HPACK
compression format. Supports indexed header fields, literal header
fields with and without indexing, and dynamic table size updates.

Huffman encoding is NOT used for encoding (literal strings only).
Huffman decoding is not implemented in this initial version; attempts
to decode Huffman-encoded strings will return an error.

# Example

```tml
use std::http::h2::hpack::{HpackContext, hpack_encode_headers, hpack_decode_headers}

var ctx = HpackContext::new(4096)
let encoded = hpack_encode_headers(mut ref ctx, headers)
```
