modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
HTTP/2 protocol support (RFC 7540 + RFC 7541).

Provides binary frame codec, HPACK header compression, stream state
machine, and connection management for HTTP/2.

modules.name: server
modules.doc:
HTTP/2 server integration — bridges H2Connection to the App framework.

The H2Server reads raw bytes from a socket, decodes frames, processes
them through H2Connection, and dispatches requests to the application
handler. Responses are encoded as HTTP/2 frames and sent back.

# Usage

This module is designed to be called from the HTTP server's connection
handler when an HTTP/2 connection is detected (via ALPN or connection
preface). It handles:
  1. Connection preface validation
  2. SETTINGS exchange
  3. Frame decode/dispatch loop
  4. Response encoding (HEADERS + DATA frames)
modules.summary: HTTP/2 server integration — bridges H2Connection to the App framework.

modules.name: stream
modules.doc:
HTTP/2 stream state machine (RFC 7540 Section 5.1).

Each HTTP/2 stream has a lifecycle defined by a state machine.
Frames cause transitions between states; invalid transitions produce
protocol errors.

Stream IDs: odd = client-initiated, even = server-initiated, 0 = connection.

# Design Note

H2Stream is a pure scalar struct (no Buffer/pointer fields) so it can
safely be stored in raw memory via ptr_read/ptr_write. Header block
accumulation is handled by the connection layer, which owns the Buffers.

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
HTTP — complete HTTP/1.1 stack with NestJS-style framework.

## Module Structure

| Module | Contents |
|--------|----------|
| `protocol` | method, status, version, headers, error, cookie, chunked, functions |
| `server` | HTTP server, workers, IOCP, dispatch, parsing, connections |
| `client` | HTTP client, agent, connection pool |
| `request` | request/response types, body parser, content type, multipart, encoding |
| `middleware` | CORS, security, ETag, cache, rate limit, compression, SSE, static files |
| `router` | radix-tree URL router |
| `app` | application framework, controller, arena |
| `websocket` | WebSocket protocol (RFC 6455) |
| `h2` | HTTP/2 protocol (RFC 7540 + RFC 7541) |
| `framework` | NestJS-style: JsonResponse, guards, pipes, interceptors |
modules.summary: HTTP — complete HTTP/1.1 stack with NestJS-style framework.

modules.name: chunked
modules.doc:
HTTP chunked transfer encoding — read and write.

Implements chunked transfer encoding per RFC 7230 Section 4.1.
Used when the total content length is unknown at the time headers are sent.

Format:
  chunk-size (hex)\r\n
  chunk-data\r\n
  ...
  0\r\n
  trailer-headers\r\n
  \r\n

items.summary: Decodes a chunked transfer-encoded body.

items.name: recv_chunked_body
items.signature: func recv_chunked_body(fd: I64, initial_data: Str, body_limit: I64) -> Str
items.doc:
Reads a chunked transfer-encoded body from a socket.

`fd` is the socket file descriptor. `initial_data` is any leftover data
after the \r\n\r\n header terminator that was already read from the socket.
`body_limit` is the maximum allowed body size (0 means use MAX_CHUNKED_BODY).

Returns the decoded body as Str, or "" if decoding fails or body exceeds limit.

This function handles the case where chunk boundaries may span multiple
recv() calls, accumulating raw data in a Buffer and periodically attempting
to decode the accumulated chunked stream.

items.name: Headers
items.doc:
A collection of HTTP headers with case-insensitive key lookup.

Internally backed by a `HashMap[Str, Str]`. Keys are lowercased on every
operation so that lookups are case-insensitive per HTTP semantics.

The handle field stores the HashMap's internal *Unit pointer directly.
This avoids embedding a generic type in the struct (which causes
cross-module monomorphization bugs). Operations construct a temporary
HashMap, call the method, then null out the temporary's handle via
lowlevel to prevent the auto-Drop from freeing the shared storage.
items.summary: A collection of HTTP headers with case-insensitive key lookup.

modules.name: router
modules.doc:
Radix tree HTTP router — pure TML implementation.

High-performance URL router using a compressed radix tree (one per HTTP method).
Inspired by find-my-way. Supports static routes, path parameters (`:param`),
and wildcard catch-all routes (`*`).

# Example

```tml
use std::http::router::router::{Router, RouteMatch}

let router = Router::new()
router.on("GET", "/users/:id", 1)
router.on("GET", "/users/:id/posts", 2)
router.on("POST", "/users", 3)
router.on("GET", "/files/*filepath", 4)

let m = router.find("GET", "/users/42/posts")
assert(m.found)
assert_eq(m.handler_id, 2)
assert_eq(m.get_param("id"), "42")
m.destroy()
router.destroy()
```
modules.summary: Radix tree HTTP router — pure TML implementation.

modules.name: iocp_worker
modules.doc:
IOCP-based HTTP server worker — Windows-native async I/O.

Uses Windows I/O Completion Ports for maximum throughput:
  - Create IOCP handle, associate listening socket
  - Pre-issue N AcceptEx operations (async accept pool)
  - N worker threads each call tml_iocp_wait() in a loop
  - Completions: accept → recv → parse/dispatch → send → keepalive/close

Connection state is managed in a flat array indexed by token.
Each token maps to a connection slot with socket, recv/send buffers, and state.
modules.summary: IOCP-based HTTP server worker — Windows-native async I/O.

items.doc:

Each worker calls tml_iocp_wait() in a blocking loop, processing completions.

items.summary: Worker thread function for IOCP event loop. Each worker calls tml_iocp_wait() in a blocking loop, processing completions. Multiple workers on the same IOCP handle is the correct Windows pattern.

modules.name: worker
modules.doc:
HTTP server workers — thread pool and event loop implementations.

Two server modes:
  - Thread pool (`app_listen`): N worker threads pull connections from a shared queue.
    Each worker handles one connection at a time (blocking I/O). Best throughput.
  - Event loop (`app_listen_evloop`): N workers each own a non-blocking poller.
    Accept thread distributes connections round-robin. More concurrent connections.

Both modes share the same shared-state memory layout and dispatch pipeline.
modules.summary: HTTP server workers — thread pool and event loop implementations.

Phase 3: Force shutdown remaining connections.

modules.name: work_stealing
modules.doc:
Work-stealing scheduler for HTTP thread pool.

Each worker has a local LIFO queue (for cache locality).
Overflow goes to the global FIFO queue.
Idle workers steal from other workers' local queues.

Based on Tokio's scheduler design:
- LIFO local queue: new connections processed immediately (hot cache)
- FIFO global queue: overflow from full local queues
- Steal-half: idle workers take half of a busy worker's local queue
modules.summary: Work-stealing scheduler for HTTP thread pool.

items.name: ws_accept_key
items.doc:
Computes the Sec-WebSocket-Accept key from the client's Sec-WebSocket-Key.

Per RFC 6455 Section 4.2.2:
1. Concatenate the client key with the GUID
2. Take the SHA-1 hash
3. Base64-encode the result

# Examples

```tml
// RFC 6455 Section 4.2.2 test vector
let accept = ws_accept_key("dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==")
assert(accept == "s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=")
```

This module implements the core backward pass that traverses the computation

modules.name: graph
modules.doc:
Tape-based computation graph for automatic differentiation.

The autograd engine uses a linear tape that records operations in
forward-execution order.  During the backward pass the tape is
traversed in reverse to propagate gradients from outputs back to
leaf variables.

# Design

Operations and their outputs are stored in two parallel lists
(`ops` and `outputs`) indexed by the same tape position.  This
avoids issues with storing compound structs inside generic `List[T]`
containers and keeps the layout simple and cache-friendly.
modules.summary: Tape-based computation graph for automatic differentiation.

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
Automatic differentiation engine.

Provides tape-based reverse-mode automatic differentiation (backpropagation)
for the IA tensor library.

# Modules

| Module     | Description                                      |
|------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| `variable` | [`Variable`] — tensor wrapper with grad tracking  |
| `graph`    | [`Tape`] — computation tape and operation encoding |

modules.name: variable
modules.doc:
Variable — a tensor wrapper that tracks computation for automatic differentiation.

A Variable wraps a Tensor and records whether it requires gradient
computation.  When operations are performed on Variables while a Tape
is recording, the operation is logged so that `backward()` can later
traverse the computation graph in reverse to compute gradients.
modules.summary: Variable — a tensor wrapper that tracks computation for automatic differentiation.

items.name: Variable
items.doc:
A tensor that participates in automatic differentiation.

Variables track their creation operation so that gradients can be
computed by traversing the computation graph in reverse.

TML AI Library (IA)

Tensor operations, neural networks, and machine learning primitives.

modules.name: activation
modules.doc:
Activation functions for neural networks.

All functions take a tensor by reference and return a new tensor of
the same shape.  Element-wise operations use F64x2 SIMD where possible.

items.name: relu
items.doc:
Rectified Linear Unit: `max(0, x)`.

Returns a new tensor of the same shape where negative values are zeroed.
items.summary: Rectified Linear Unit: `max(0, x)`.

items.name: leaky_relu
items.signature: func leaky_relu(input: ref Tensor, alpha: F64) -> Tensor
items.doc:
Leaky ReLU: `x` if `x > 0`, else `alpha * x`.

Default alpha is typically 0.01.
items.summary: Leaky ReLU: `x` if `x > 0`, else `alpha * x`.

items.name: sigmoid
items.doc: Sigmoid activation: `1 / (1 + exp(-x))`.
items.summary: Sigmoid activation: `1 / (1 + exp(-x))`.

items.name: tanh_act
items.doc:
Hyperbolic tangent activation: `(exp(x) - exp(-x)) / (exp(x) + exp(-x))`.

Named `tanh_act` to avoid shadowing any built-in `tanh`.
items.summary: Hyperbolic tangent activation: `(exp(x) - exp(-x)) / (exp(x) + exp(-x))`.

items.name: gelu
items.doc:
GELU activation (tanh approximation):

`x * 0.5 * (1 + tanh(sqrt(2/pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x^3)))`

This is the approximation used in GPT-2, BERT, and most transformers.
items.summary: GELU activation (tanh approximation):

items.name: silu
items.doc: SiLU (Sigmoid Linear Unit) / Swish activation: `x * sigmoid(x)`.
items.summary: SiLU (Sigmoid Linear Unit) / Swish activation: `x * sigmoid(x)`.

items.name: softmax
items.doc:
Softmax over the entire 1-D tensor, or along the last dimension for 2-D.

`softmax(x_i) = exp(x_i - max(x)) / sum(exp(x_j - max(x)))`

The max subtraction ensures numerical stability.
items.summary: Softmax over the entire 1-D tensor, or along the last dimension for 2-D.

items.name: log_softmax
items.doc:
Log-softmax: `log(softmax(x))` computed in a numerically stable way.

`log_softmax(x_i) = x_i - max(x) - log(sum(exp(x_j - max(x))))`
items.summary: Log-softmax: `log(softmax(x))` computed in a numerically stable way.

modules.name: attention
modules.doc:
Attention mechanisms for transformer architectures.

Provides scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention.
All operations work on 2-D tensors `[seq_len, embed_dim]` (single batch).

items.name: scaled_dot_product_attention
items.signature: func scaled_dot_product_attention(query: ref Tensor, key: ref Tensor, value: ref Tensor) -> IaResult[Tensor]
items.doc:
Scaled dot-product attention (Vaswani et al., 2017).

`Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q @ K^T / sqrt(d_k)) @ V`

* `query`:  `[seq_q, d_k]`
* `key`:    `[seq_k, d_k]`
* `value`:  `[seq_k, d_v]`
* Returns:  `[seq_q, d_v]`
items.summary: Scaled dot-product attention (Vaswani et al., 2017).

items.name: MultiHeadAttention
items.doc:
Multi-head attention layer.

Splits the embedding into `num_heads` heads, applies scaled dot-product
attention to each head independently, then concatenates and projects.

* `embed_dim` — total embedding dimension (must be divisible by `num_heads`).
* `num_heads` — number of attention heads.
* `head_dim` — per-head dimension (`embed_dim / num_heads`).
items.summary: Multi-head attention layer.

methods.name: new
methods.signature: func new(embed_dim: I64, num_heads: I64) -> MultiHeadAttention
methods.doc:
Create a new multi-head attention layer.

`embed_dim` must be divisible by `num_heads`.
methods.summary: Create a new multi-head attention layer.

methods.name: forward
methods.signature: func forward(this, query: ref Tensor, key: ref Tensor, value: ref Tensor) -> IaResult[Tensor]
methods.doc:
Forward pass: multi-head self-attention.

For self-attention, pass the same tensor for query, key, and value.
For cross-attention, query comes from the decoder, key/value from the encoder.

* `query`:  `[seq_q, embed_dim]`
* `key`:    `[seq_k, embed_dim]`
* `value`:  `[seq_k, embed_dim]`
* Returns:  `[seq_q, embed_dim]`
methods.summary: Forward pass: multi-head self-attention.

modules.name: dropout
modules.doc:
Dropout regularisation layer.

During training, randomly zeroes elements with probability `p` and scales
surviving elements by `1/(1-p)` (inverted dropout).  During evaluation,
the input passes through unchanged.

items.name: Dropout
items.doc:
Dropout layer — randomly zeroes elements during training.

* `p` — probability of zeroing each element (typically 0.1–0.5).
* `training` — whether the layer is in training mode.

Uses inverted dropout: surviving elements are scaled by `1/(1-p)`
so that no scaling is needed at inference time.
items.summary: Dropout layer — randomly zeroes elements during training.

Fully-connected (dense) linear layer: `y = x @ W + b`.

The weight matrix is stored as `[in_features, out_features]` so the
forward pass is simply `input @ weight + bias` — no transpose needed.

modules.name: loss
modules.doc:
Loss functions for neural network training.

Each function takes prediction and target tensors of the same shape
and returns a scalar (1-element) tensor representing the loss.
modules.summary: Loss functions for neural network training.

items.name: mse_loss
items.signature: func mse_loss(predictions: ref Tensor, targets: ref Tensor) -> Tensor
items.doc:
Mean Squared Error loss: `mean((predictions - targets)^2)`.

Both tensors must have the same number of elements.
items.summary: Mean Squared Error loss: `mean((predictions - targets)^2)`.

items.name: cross_entropy_loss
items.signature: func cross_entropy_loss(predictions: ref Tensor, targets: ref Tensor) -> Tensor
items.doc:
Cross-entropy loss for probability distributions.

`loss = -mean(sum_classes(targets * log(predictions + eps)))` per sample.

For soft labels (one-hot or probability targets) over `[batch, classes]`
or `[classes]`.  A small epsilon (1e-12) prevents log(0).
items.summary: Cross-entropy loss for probability distributions.

items.name: l1_loss
items.signature: func l1_loss(predictions: ref Tensor, targets: ref Tensor) -> Tensor
items.doc: L1 (Mean Absolute Error) loss: `mean(|predictions - targets|)`.
items.summary: L1 (Mean Absolute Error) loss: `mean(|predictions - targets|)`.

items.name: bce_loss
items.signature: func bce_loss(predictions: ref Tensor, targets: ref Tensor) -> Tensor
items.doc:
Binary cross-entropy loss: `-mean(y * log(p) + (1-y) * log(1-p))`.

Predictions should be in [0, 1] (e.g. sigmoid output).
Targets should be 0 or 1.
items.summary: Binary cross-entropy loss: `-mean(y * log(p) + (1-y) * log(1-p))`.

items.name: huber_loss
items.signature: func huber_loss(predictions: ref Tensor, targets: ref Tensor, delta: F64) -> Tensor
items.doc:
Huber loss (Smooth L1): quadratic for small errors, linear for large.

`loss = 0.5 * x^2  if |x| <= delta`
`loss = delta * (|x| - 0.5 * delta)  otherwise`
items.summary: Huber loss (Smooth L1): quadratic for small errors, linear for large.

Neural network module primitives.

Provides the [`Parameter`] type for learnable weights, and weight
initialization functions (Xavier/Glorot, Kaiming/He).

items.doc:
A learnable parameter — a named tensor that participates in training.

Parameters wrap a tensor and a human-readable name so that layers
can expose their weights for optimiser updates and serialisation.

items.name: xavier_uniform
items.signature: func xavier_uniform(fan_in: I64, fan_out: I64) -> Tensor
items.doc:
Xavier (Glorot) uniform initialisation.

Creates an F64 tensor of shape `[fan_in, fan_out]` with values drawn
uniformly from `[-limit, limit]` where `limit = sqrt(6 / (fan_in + fan_out))`.
items.summary: Xavier (Glorot) uniform initialisation.

items.name: kaiming_uniform
items.signature: func kaiming_uniform(fan_in: I64, fan_out: I64) -> Tensor
items.doc:
Kaiming (He) uniform initialisation — designed for ReLU networks.

Creates an F64 tensor of shape `[fan_in, fan_out]` with values drawn
uniformly from `[-limit, limit]` where `limit = sqrt(6 / fan_in)`.
items.summary: Kaiming (He) uniform initialisation — designed for ReLU networks.

items.name: xavier_normal
items.signature: func xavier_normal(fan_in: I64, fan_out: I64) -> Tensor
items.doc:
Xavier (Glorot) normal initialisation.

Creates an F64 tensor of shape `[fan_in, fan_out]` with values drawn
from N(0, std) where `std = sqrt(2 / (fan_in + fan_out))`.
items.summary: Xavier (Glorot) normal initialisation.

items.name: kaiming_normal
items.signature: func kaiming_normal(fan_in: I64, fan_out: I64) -> Tensor
items.doc:
Kaiming (He) normal initialisation.

Creates an F64 tensor of shape `[fan_in, fan_out]` with values drawn
from N(0, std) where `std = sqrt(2 / fan_in)`.
items.summary: Kaiming (He) normal initialisation.

modules.name: norm
modules.doc:
Normalisation layers: LayerNorm and RMSNorm.

Both operate on 2-D tensors `[batch, dim]` and normalise along the
last dimension (each row independently).

items.name: LayerNorm
items.doc:
Layer Normalisation (Ba et al., 2016).

For each row (sample) in a `[batch, dim]` tensor, normalises to zero
mean and unit variance, then applies a learnable affine transform:

`output = gamma * (x - mean) / sqrt(var + eps) + beta`

Fields:
* `normalized_shape` — size of the last dimension.

items.name: CosineAnnealing
items.doc:
Cosine annealing scheduler.

Learning rate follows a cosine curve from `lr_max` down to `lr_min`
over `total_steps` steps:

```
lr = lr_min + 0.5 * (lr_max - lr_min) * (1 + cos(pi * step / total_steps))
```

Linear warmup scheduler.

Learning rate increases linearly from 0 to `base_lr` over
`warmup_steps` steps. After warmup, returns `base_lr`.

```

```

Stochastic Gradient Descent with momentum and weight decay.

Implements classical SGD with optional Nesterov-style momentum

items.name: SGD
items.doc:
Stochastic Gradient Descent optimizer.

Supports momentum and weight decay. The update rule is:

```
if weight_decay > 0: grad = grad + weight_decay * param
if momentum > 0:
    velocity = momentum * velocity + grad
    update = velocity
else:
    update = grad
param = param - lr * update
```
items.summary: Stochastic Gradient Descent optimizer.

- `weight_decay`: L2 regularization coefficient (0.0 = none)

Element-wise comparison functions return F64 tensors where 1.0 represents

All binary comparison functions support NumPy-style broadcasting via the
same `broadcast_shape` infrastructure used by `ops.tml`.

items.name: where_cond
items.signature: func where_cond(cond: ref Tensor, a: ref Tensor, b: ref Tensor) -> IaResult[Tensor]
items.doc:
Element-wise conditional selection.

For each element position `i`:
```
result[i] = cond[i] != 0.0 ? a[i] : b[i]
```

All three tensors (`cond`, `a`, `b`) must have the same shape.
Broadcasting is NOT applied — shapes must match exactly to keep semantics
unambiguous.

# Errors
Returns `IaError::ShapeMismatch` if any of the three shapes differ.

modules.doc:
Tensor indexing and slicing operations.

Provides slice, gather, and scatter operations following NumPy/PyTorch
semantics.

items.name: slice
items.signature: func slice(a: ref Tensor, dim: I64, start: I64, end: I64) -> IaResult[Tensor]
items.doc:
Extract a sub-tensor along dimension `dim` from index `start` (inclusive)
to `end` (exclusive).

The result has the same rank as `a`.  Dimension `dim` has size `end - start`;
all other dimensions are unchanged.

For a tensor of shape [d0, d1, d2] with `dim=1`, `start=1`, `end=3`:
- Output shape: [d0, 2, d2]
- Output[i, j, k] = Input[i, start + j, k]

# Errors
- `IaError::InvalidAxis` if `dim` is out of range.
- `IaError::IndexOutOfBounds` if `start` or `end` are out of range, or
  `start >= end`.
items.summary: Extract a sub-tensor along dimension `dim` from index `start` (inclusive) to `end` (exclusive).

items.name: gather
items.signature: func gather(a: ref Tensor, dim: I64, indices: ref Tensor) -> IaResult[Tensor]
items.doc:
Gather elements from tensor `a` along dimension `dim` using `indices`.

`indices` must be a 1-D integer tensor.  The output has the same shape as
`indices`.  For each position `i` in `indices`:

```
result[i] = a.select(dim, indices[i])
```

where `select(dim, idx)` means: for every multi-dim position, replace the
`dim`-th index with `idx` and keep all other indices fixed to `i` (for 1-D
`indices`).

Concretely, when `indices` is 1-D and `a` is N-D:
- `result[i]` is the element of `a` at the position where the `dim`-th
  index equals `(I64)indices[i]` and all other indices are `i` (clamped to
  their respective dimensions).

For the common case where `a` is also 1-D this reduces to simple index
lookup: `result[i] = a[indices[i]]`.

# Errors
- `IaError::InvalidAxis` if `dim` is out of range.
- `IaError::InvalidAxis` if `indices` is not 1-D.
- `IaError::IndexOutOfBounds` if any index value is out of bounds for the
  gather dimension.
items.summary: Gather elements from tensor `a` along dimension `dim` using `indices`.

items.name: scatter
items.signature: func scatter(a: ref Tensor, dim: I64, indices: ref Tensor, src: ref Tensor) -> IaResult[Tensor]
items.doc:
Scatter values from `src` into a copy of `a` at positions given by `indices`.

This is the inverse of `gather`.  `indices` must be a 1-D integer tensor
with the same length as `src`.  For each position `i`:

```
result[...gather position for indices[i]...] = src[i]
```

The positions follow the same mapping as `gather`: the `dim`-th index of
the destination is `(I64)indices[i]`, and all other indices are derived
from `i` (clamped to dimension bounds).

# Errors
- `IaError::InvalidAxis` if `dim` is out of range.
- `IaError::InvalidAxis` if `indices` or `src` are not 1-D.
- `IaError::ShapeMismatch` if `indices.numel() != src.numel()`.
- `IaError::IndexOutOfBounds` if any index value is out of bounds.
items.summary: Scatter values from `src` into a copy of `a` at positions given by `indices`.

modules.name: matmul
modules.doc:
Matrix multiplication for tensors.

Provides both a naive triple-loop implementation and a cache-friendly
blocked (tiled) variant for better performance on large matrices.
Inner loops use F64x2 SIMD (128-bit SSE2) to process 2 F64 elements
per iteration, with a scalar tail for odd-length dimensions.

items.name: matmul
items.signature: func matmul(a: ref Tensor, b: ref Tensor) -> IaResult[Tensor]
items.doc:
Multiply two 2-D tensors: a[M, K] @ b[K, N] → result[M, N].

Both tensors must be rank 2 and their inner dimensions must match
(a.dim(1) == b.dim(0)).  The result dtype matches `a`.
items.summary: Multiply two 2-D tensors: a[M, K] @ b[K, N] → result[M, N].

items.name: matmul_blocked
items.signature: func matmul_blocked(a: ref Tensor, b: ref Tensor, block_size: I64) -> IaResult[Tensor]
items.doc:
Cache-friendly blocked (tiled) matrix multiplication.

Produces the same result as `matmul` but processes data in tiles of
`block_size × block_size` to improve cache utilisation on large matrices.

`block_size` must be > 0.  A value of 64 is a reasonable default.
items.summary: Cache-friendly blocked (tiled) matrix multiplication.

modules.name: reshape
modules.doc:
Tensor reshaping and dimension manipulation.

Provides reshape, transpose, permute, squeeze, unsqueeze, expand, and
contiguous operations following NumPy/PyTorch semantics.

items.name: reshape
items.signature: func reshape(a: ref Tensor, new_dims: List[I64]) -> IaResult[Tensor]
items.doc:
Reshape tensor `a` to the given dimensions.

The total number of elements must be preserved.  Data is copied in
row-major (C-contiguous) flat order, so the semantics match NumPy's
`reshape` with `order='C'`.

# Errors
Returns `IaError::ShapeMismatch` if `product(new_dims) != a.numel()`.
items.summary: Reshape tensor `a` to the given dimensions.

items.name: transpose
items.doc:
Transpose a 2-D tensor: shape [M, N] → [N, M].

Element `a[i, j]` maps to `result[j, i]`.

# Errors
Returns `IaError::InvalidAxis` if `a` is not exactly 2-D.
items.summary: Transpose a 2-D tensor: shape [M, N] → [N, M].

items.name: permute
items.signature: func permute(a: ref Tensor, axes: List[I64]) -> IaResult[Tensor]
items.doc:
Permute the dimensions of tensor `a` according to `axes`.

`axes` must be a permutation of `[0, 1, ..., rank-1]`.  The output shape
is built by selecting `a.dim(axes[i])` for each output dimension `i`.

For each output element at multi-dimensional index `out_idx`, the
corresponding input index is obtained by `in_idx[axes[i]] = out_idx[i]`.

# Errors
- `IaError::InvalidAxis` if `axes.len() != a.rank()`.
- `IaError::InvalidAxis` if `axes` is not a valid permutation.
items.summary: Permute the dimensions of tensor `a` according to `axes`.

items.name: squeeze
items.doc:
Remove all dimensions of size 1 from tensor `a`.

The data is not modified; only the shape changes.  If no dimensions of
size 1 exist, the original data is returned in a tensor with the same
shape.  If all dimensions are 1 (e.g. shape [1, 1]), the result is a
rank-1 tensor with a single element.
items.summary: Remove all dimensions of size 1 from tensor `a`.

items.name: unsqueeze
items.signature: func unsqueeze(a: ref Tensor, dim: I64) -> IaResult[Tensor]
items.doc:
Insert a dimension of size 1 at position `dim`.

`dim` must be in the range `[0, rank]` (inclusive).

# Errors
Returns `IaError::InvalidAxis` if `dim` is out of range.
items.summary: Insert a dimension of size 1 at position `dim`.

items.name: expand
items.signature: func expand(a: ref Tensor, new_dims: List[I64]) -> IaResult[Tensor]
items.doc:
Expand tensor `a` to `new_dims` using broadcasting rules.

Each dimension of `a` must either match the corresponding new dimension or
be exactly 1 (in which case the data is repeated along that axis).  The
length of `new_dims` must equal `a.rank()`.

# Errors
- `IaError::ShapeMismatch` if `new_dims.len() != a.rank()`.
- `IaError::ShapeMismatch` if a non-1 dimension does not match.
items.summary: Expand tensor `a` to `new_dims` using broadcasting rules.

items.name: contiguous
items.doc:
Return a contiguous (row-major) copy of tensor `a`.

Copies all elements in flat order into a new tensor with the same shape
and dtype.  Always produces a fresh allocation regardless of whether the
input is already contiguous.
items.summary: Return a contiguous (row-major) copy of tensor `a`.

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
String interning module.

Provides the [`Interner`] type for deduplicating strings. Each unique string
is stored once, and callers receive an opaque [`InternedStr`] handle that can
be used to retrieve the original string in O(1).

# Usage

```tml
use std::intern::{Interner, InternedStr}

let mut pool = Interner::new()
let a = pool.intern("hello")
let b = pool.intern("hello")
assert_eq(a.id(), b.id())          // same handle — deduplicated
assert_eq(pool.get(a), "hello")    // retrieve original string
```

# Design

Backed by a `HashMap[Str, I64]` for O(1) lookup-or-insert and a `List[Str]`
for O(1) index-based retrieval. The `InternedStr` handle is a thin wrapper
around an I64 index.

Path syntax:
- `.key` or `key` - access object field
- `[n]` - access array index
- Chain with dots: `users[0].name`, `data.items[2].value`

Returns Nothing if any part of the path is invalid.

# Example
```tml
let json = parse_or_panic("{\"users\": [{\"name\": \"Alice\"}]}")
when json.get_path("users[0].name") {
    Just(name) => println(name.unwrap_str()),  // "Alice"
    Nothing => println("Not found"),
}
```

modules.name: log
modules.doc:
Structured logging for TML programs.

This module provides structured logging with level-based filtering,
module tags, multiple output formats, file sinks, and structured
key-value fields.

# Log Levels

| Level | Value | Description |
|-------|-------|-------------|
| Trace | 0 | Fine-grained internal tracing |
| Debug | 1 | Debugging information |
| Info | 2 | General informational messages |
| Warn | 3 | Potential issues |
| Error | 4 | Recoverable errors |
| Fatal | 5 | Unrecoverable errors |

# Output Formats

| Format  | Value | Description |
|---------|-------|-------------|
| Text    | 0     | Human-readable text (default) |
| JSON    | 1     | Machine-parseable JSON lines |
| Compact | 2     | Short-form with 2-char levels |

# Example

```tml
use std::log

// Basic logging
log::info("app", "Server started on port 8080")
log::warn("app", "Connection pool is 80% full")
log::error("db", "Failed to connect to database")

// Structured logging with key-value fields
log::structured(log::INFO, "http", "Request handled", "method=GET;status=200;ms=42")

// Module-level filtering
log::set_filter("server=debug,db=trace,*=warn")

// File logging
log::open_file("app.log")
log::info("app", "This goes to stderr AND app.log")
log::close_file()

// JSON output format
log::set_format(log::FORMAT_JSON)

// Auto-configure from TML_LOG environment variable
log::init_from_env()
```

items.name: TRACE
items.doc: Finest-grained tracing information.
items.summary: Finest-grained tracing information.

items.name: DEBUG
items.doc: Debugging information useful during development.
items.summary: Debugging information useful during development.

items.name: INFO
items.doc: General informational messages about program progress.
items.summary: General informational messages about program progress.

items.doc: Potential issues that deserve attention.
items.summary: Potential issues that deserve attention.

items.name: ERROR
items.doc: Recoverable errors that allow the program to continue.
items.summary: Recoverable errors that allow the program to continue.

items.name: FATAL
items.doc: Unrecoverable errors that will cause the program to stop.
items.summary: Unrecoverable errors that will cause the program to stop.

items.doc: Human-readable text format (default).
items.summary: Human-readable text format (default).

items.doc: Machine-parseable JSON format (one object per line).
items.summary: Machine-parseable JSON format (one object per line).

items.doc: Compact format with 2-character level names.
items.summary: Compact format with 2-character level names.

items.name: msg
items.signature: func msg(level: I32, module: Str, message: Str)
items.doc:
Log a message at the given level with a module tag.

This is the core logging function. Prefer the level-specific
convenience functions (`trace`, `debug`, `info`, etc.) for clarity.

# Parameters

- `level`: Log level (use the constants TRACE through FATAL)
- `module`: Module tag for filtering (e.g., "app", "db", "server")
- `message`: The log message

# Example

```tml
log::msg(log::INFO, "app", "Server started")
```
items.summary: Log a message at the given level with a module tag.

items.name: trace
items.doc:
Log a message at TRACE level.

Use for fine-grained debugging information that is typically
only enabled during development.

# Example

```tml
log::trace("parser", "Entering parse_expression()")
```
items.summary: Log a message at TRACE level.

items.name: debug
items.doc:
Log a message at DEBUG level.

Use for information useful during debugging but not needed
in production.

# Example

```tml
log::debug("cache", "Cache miss for key: users")
```
items.summary: Log a message at DEBUG level.

items.name: info
items.doc:
Log a message at INFO level.

Use for general progress information about the program.

# Example

```tml
log::info("server", "Listening on port 8080")
```
items.summary: Log a message at INFO level.

items.name: warn
items.doc:
Log a message at WARN level.

Use for conditions that might cause problems but don't prevent
the program from functioning.

# Example

```tml
log::warn("pool", "Connection pool utilization at 90%")
```
items.summary: Log a message at WARN level.

items.name: error
items.doc:
Log a message at ERROR level.

Use for errors that are recoverable but indicate something
went wrong.

# Example

```tml
log::error("db", "Query failed, retrying...")
```
items.summary: Log a message at ERROR level.

items.name: fatal
items.doc:
Log a message at FATAL level.

Use for unrecoverable errors. The program should typically
exit after logging at this level.

# Example

```tml
log::fatal("app", "Cannot open configuration file")
```
items.summary: Log a message at FATAL level.

items.name: set_level
items.doc:
Set the minimum log level.

Messages below this level will be silently discarded.
Default is WARN (3).

# Example

```tml
// Show all messages including debug
log::set_level(log::DEBUG)

// Only show errors and fatal
log::set_level(log::ERROR)
```
items.summary: Set the minimum log level.

items.name: get_level
items.doc:
Get the current minimum log level.

# Example

```tml
let current = log::get_level()
```
items.summary: Get the current minimum log level.

items.name: enabled
items.summary: Check if a message at the given level would be logged.

items.name: set_filter
items.doc:
Set a module-level filter specification.

Format: "module1=level,module2=level,*=default_level"

Each module can have its own log level. The wildcard `*` sets the
default level for modules not explicitly listed. Module names
without `=level` are set to TRACE (show everything).

# Example

```tml
// Only show debug from server, trace from db, warn for everything else
log::set_filter("server=debug,db=trace,*=warn")

// Show everything from a specific module
log::set_filter("mymodule")
```
items.summary: Set a module-level filter specification.

items.name: module_enabled
items.signature: func module_enabled(level: I32, module: Str) -> Bool
items.doc:
Check if a message at the given level from a specific module would be logged.

Unlike `enabled()`, this respects per-module filter overrides set
via `set_filter()`.

# Example

```tml
log::set_filter("db=trace,*=warn")
assert(log::module_enabled(log::TRACE, "db"))   // true
assert(not log::module_enabled(log::TRACE, "app"))  // false (default=warn)
```
items.summary: Check if a message at the given level from a specific module would be logged.

items.name: structured
items.signature: func structured(level: I32, module: Str, message: Str, fields: Str)
items.doc:
Log a structured message with key-value fields.

Fields are passed as a semicolon-separated string of key=value pairs.
When the output format is JSON, fields become JSON properties.
In text format, fields are appended after a ` | ` separator.

# Parameters

- `level`: Log level
- `module`: Module tag
- `message`: The log message
- `fields`: Semicolon-separated key=value pairs

# Example

```tml
log::structured(log::INFO, "http", "Request handled", "method=GET;status=200;ms=42")

// Text output:  INFO [http] Request handled | method=GET;status=200;ms=42
// JSON output:  {"level":"INFO","module":"http","msg":"Request handled","method":"GET","status":"200","ms":"42"}
```
items.summary: Log a structured message with key-value fields.

items.name: set_format
items.doc:
Set the log output format.

- `FORMAT_TEXT` (0): Human-readable text (default)
- `FORMAT_JSON` (1): Machine-parseable JSON lines
- `FORMAT_COMPACT` (2): Compact format with 2-char levels

# Example

```tml
log::set_format(log::FORMAT_JSON)
log::info("app", "This will be JSON")
// Output: {"level":"INFO","module":"app","msg":"This will be JSON"}
```
items.summary: Set the log output format.

items.name: get_format
items.doc:
Get the current log output format.

Returns FORMAT_TEXT (0), FORMAT_JSON (1), or FORMAT_COMPACT (2).
items.summary: Get the current log output format.

items.name: open_file
items.doc:
Open a file for log output.

All subsequent log messages will be written to both stderr and the
specified file. The file is opened in append mode.

Returns `true` on success, `false` on failure (e.g., invalid path).

# Example

```tml
if log::open_file("app.log") {
    log::info("app", "Logging to file")
    log::close_file()
}
```
items.summary: Open a file for log output.

items.name: close_file
items.doc:
Close the file sink, if one is open.

After calling this, log messages will only go to stderr
(or through the callback if one is set).
items.summary: Close the file sink, if one is open.

items.name: init_from_env
items.doc:
Configure logging from the TML_LOG environment variable.

Reads the `TML_LOG` environment variable and applies it:
- If it contains a simple level name (e.g., "debug"), sets the global level
- If it contains a filter spec (e.g., "server=debug,*=warn"), applies module filters

Returns `true` if `TML_LOG` was found and applied, `false` otherwise.

# Example

```tml
// At program startup:
log::init_from_env()

// If TML_LOG=debug is set, all modules show debug and above
// If TML_LOG=server=trace,*=warn is set, per-module filtering is applied
```
items.summary: Configure logging from the TML_LOG environment variable.

modules.name: math
modules.doc:
Mathematical functions and constants.

This module provides common mathematical operations for floating-point
numbers. It wraps LLVM intrinsics for basic operations and uses libc
FFI for transcendental functions.

# Constants

| Constant | Value | Description |
|----------|-------|-------------|
| [`PI`] | 3.14159... | Ratio of circumference to diameter |
| [`E`] | 2.71828... | Euler's number |
| [`TAU`] | 6.28318... | 2 * PI |
| [`SQRT_2`] | 1.41421... | Square root of 2 |
| [`LN_2`] | 0.69314... | Natural log of 2 |
| [`LN_10`] | 2.30258... | Natural log of 10 |

# Functions (F64)

## Trigonometric
`sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2`

## Hyperbolic
`sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`

## Exponential & Logarithmic
`exp`, `ln`, `log2`, `log10`, `pow`

## Rounding
`floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `trunc`

## Utility
`abs`, `sqrt`, `cbrt`, `hypot`, `min`, `max`, `clamp`
`to_radians`, `to_degrees`, `mul_add`, `fract`, `copysign`, `signum`

# F32 Variants

All functions have F32 variants with a `_f32` suffix:
`sin_f32`, `cos_f32`, `sqrt_f32`, `mul_add_f32`, etc.

The TML Standard Library.

This library provides common functionality for TML programs, including
collections, I/O, networking, string manipulation, and error handling.

# Modules

| Module | Description |

items.name: UdpHandle
items.doc:
A UDP socket integrated with the event loop.

Provides callback-based async UDP operations via the EventLoop for
handling multiple datagram sources efficiently.

# Examples

```tml
use std::aio::EventLoop
use std::net::UdpHandle
use std::net::{SocketAddr, SocketAddrV4, Ipv4Addr}

let mut loop: EventLoop = EventLoop::new()
let ip: Ipv4Addr = Ipv4Addr::new(127, 0, 0, 1)
let addr: SocketAddr = SocketAddr::V4(SocketAddrV4::new(ip, 8000))
let mut handle: UdpHandle = UdpHandle::bind(loop as I64, addr)!
handle.set_on_message(on_message_fn as I64)
handle.register(ref loop)
loop.run()
handle.close(ref loop)
loop.destroy()
```

modules.name: buffer_view
modules.doc:
Zero-copy byte buffer view for efficient network I/O.

`BufferView` provides a lightweight, non-owning view into a contiguous
byte region. It enables zero-copy parsing and slicing of network data
without allocating new buffers.

# Design

`BufferView` is intentionally simple — it stores a raw pointer, an offset,
and a length. It does NOT own the underlying memory. The caller must
ensure the source data remains valid for the lifetime of the view.

# Example

```tml
use std::net::buffer_view::BufferView

// Create from a raw pointer (e.g., from a Buffer or network recv)
let view = BufferView::from_raw(data_ptr, 0, 100)
let header = view.slice(0, 12)   // First 12 bytes
let payload = view.slice(12, 100) // Remaining bytes
let byte = view.get(0)            // First byte
```
modules.summary: Zero-copy byte buffer view for efficient network I/O.

items.name: BufferView
items.doc:
A zero-copy, non-owning view into a contiguous byte region.

`BufferView` is a lightweight struct that references a byte range without
copying or owning the underlying data. This makes it ideal for parsing
network protocol headers and payloads without allocation.

# Safety

The underlying data must remain valid and unmodified for the entire
lifetime of the `BufferView`. The view does NOT own the memory and
will NOT free it on destruction.
items.summary: A zero-copy, non-owning view into a contiguous byte region.

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
Networking primitives for IP communication.

This module provides platform-independent network types for working with
IP addresses, socket addresses, and network I/O buffers.

# IP Addresses

- [`Ipv4Addr`] - A 32-bit IPv4 address (e.g., `192.168.1.1`)
- [`Ipv6Addr`] - A 128-bit IPv6 address (e.g., `::1`)
- [`IpAddr`] - An enum that can hold either IPv4 or IPv6

# Socket Addresses

Socket addresses combine an IP address with a port number:

- [`SocketAddrV4`] - IPv4 address + port
- [`SocketAddrV6`] - IPv6 address + port + flow info + scope ID
- [`SocketAddr`] - An enum that can hold either V4 or V6

# Buffer Management

Efficient buffer types for network I/O:

- [`Buffer`] - A growable byte buffer with capacity management
- [`BufferView`] - A zero-copy view into byte data
- [`BufferPool`] - Pre-allocated buffer pool for reuse

# Platform Abstraction

Low-level socket operations (in [`sys`] module):

- [`RawSocket`] - Platform-specific socket handle
- Socket creation, binding, listening, connecting
- Non-blocking I/O support

# Examples

## Working with IP Addresses

```tml
use std::net::{Ipv4Addr, Ipv6Addr, IpAddr}

// Create IPv4 addresses
let localhost = Ipv4Addr::new(127, 0, 0, 1)
let private = Ipv4Addr::new(192, 168, 1, 1)

// Use predefined constants
let loopback = Ipv4Addr::LOCALHOST
let any = Ipv4Addr::UNSPECIFIED

// Check address properties
assert(localhost.is_loopback())
assert(private.is_private())
```

## Working with Socket Addresses

```tml
use std::net::{SocketAddr, SocketAddrV4, Ipv4Addr}

// Create a socket address
let addr = SocketAddrV4::new(Ipv4Addr::LOCALHOST, 8080)

// Access components
let ip = addr.ip()
let port = addr.port()

// Or use the unified SocketAddr type
let socket: SocketAddr = SocketAddr::V4(addr)
```

## Using Buffers

```tml
use std::net::buffer::{Buffer, BufferPool}

// Use a buffer pool for efficient allocation
let pool = BufferPool::new(16, 4096)
let mut buf = pool.get()

// Write and read data
buf.write_bytes(b"Hello")
let view = buf.as_view()

// Return to pool
pool.put(buf)
```

# TCP Networking

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) types for reliable connections:

- [`TcpListener`] - Listens for incoming TCP connections
- [`TcpStream`] - A connected TCP socket for reading and writing
- [`TcpBuilder`] - Builder pattern for TCP socket configuration

# UDP Networking

UDP (User Datagram Protocol) types for connectionless communication:

- [`UdpSocket`] - A UDP socket for sending and receiving datagrams
- [`UdpBuilder`] - Builder pattern for UDP socket configuration

# TLS/SSL

Transport Layer Security for encrypted connections:

- [`TlsContext`] - TLS configuration (certificates, protocol versions)
- [`TlsStream`] - An encrypted connection wrapping a TCP stream
- [`TlsVersion`] - TLS protocol version constants
- [`TlsVerifyMode`] - Certificate verification modes

# Module Structure

- [`ip`] - IP address types (`Ipv4Addr`, `Ipv6Addr`, `IpAddr`)
- [`socket`] - Socket address types (`SocketAddrV4`, `SocketAddrV6`, `SocketAddr`)
- [`parser`] - Parsing utilities for addresses
- [`error`] - Network error types (`NetError`, `NetErrorKind`)
- [`buffer`] - Buffer management (`Buffer`, `BufferView`, `BufferPool`)
- [`sys`] - Platform abstraction layer for sockets
- [`tls`] - TLS/SSL encrypted connections
- [`async_tcp`] - Async TCP (non-blocking I/O)
- [`async_udp`] - Async UDP (non-blocking I/O with EventLoop integration)

items.name: TcpListener
items.doc:
A TCP socket server, listening for connections.

After creating a `TcpListener` by binding it to a socket address, it listens
for incoming TCP connections. These can be accepted by calling [`accept()`]
or by iterating over the [`incoming()`] iterator.

The socket will be closed when the value is dropped.
items.summary: A TCP socket server, listening for connections.

methods.name: incoming
methods.doc:
Returns an iterator over incoming connections.

Each call to `next()` on the returned iterator will block until
a new connection is accepted.


modules.name: udp
modules.doc:
UDP networking primitives.

This module provides UDP socket types for connectionless, datagram-based
communication.

# Types

- [`UdpSocket`] - A UDP socket for sending and receiving datagrams

# UDP vs TCP

UDP (User Datagram Protocol) differs from TCP in several ways:

- **Connectionless**: No connection establishment; send to any address
- **Unreliable**: Packets may be lost, duplicated, or arrive out of order
- **Message-oriented**: Each send/receive is a discrete message
- **Lower latency**: No connection overhead or retransmission delays

modules.name: interfaces
modules.doc:
C#-style OOP interfaces for class-based programming.

This module provides common interfaces for object-oriented programming,
following C# and .NET conventions.

# Core Interfaces

| Interface | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [`IEquatable[T]`] | Type-specific equality comparison |
| [`IComparable[T]`] | Type-specific ordering comparison |
| [`IHashable`] | Hash code generation |
| [`IFormattable`] | String formatting support |
| [`ICloneable`] | Object cloning |
| [`IDisposable`] | Resource cleanup |

# Collection Interfaces

| Interface | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [`IEnumerable[T]`] | Iteration support |
| [`IEnumerator[T]`] | Iterator state |
| [`ICollection[T]`] | Mutable collection |
| [`IList[T]`] | Indexed collection |
| [`IDictionary[K, V]`] | Key-value collection |
| [`IReadOnlyCollection[T]`] | Immutable collection view |

# Observer Pattern

| Interface | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| [`IObserver[T]`] | Receives notifications |
| [`IObservable[T]`] | Publishes notifications |
modules.summary: C#-style OOP interfaces for class-based programming.

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
Object-oriented programming support for TML.

This module provides C#-style OOP primitives that complement TML's native
behavior system. Use these when building class hierarchies with inheritance,
virtual dispatch, and interface contracts.

# Modules

| Module | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| [`interfaces`] | C#-style interfaces (IEquatable, IComparable, IDisposable, etc.) |
| [`object`] | Base `Object` class for class hierarchies |

# When to Use

- Use **behaviors** (`PartialEq`, `Ord`, `Hash` from `core`) for generic,
  composable abstractions following TML idioms.
- Use **interfaces** and **Object** from this module when modeling class
  hierarchies with inheritance and virtual dispatch.

modules.name: object
modules.doc:
Object base class for TML's class hierarchy.

This module provides the root `Object` class that all classes inherit from,
following C#'s System.Object pattern.

# Main Types

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`Object`] | Base class for all TML classes |
| [`Objects`] | Static utility methods for object operations |

# The Object Class

Every class in TML implicitly inherits from `Object` if no explicit base
class is specified. `Object` provides fundamental methods:

- `equals()` - Check equality by reference or value
- `get_hash_code()` - Return a hash code for the object
- `to_string()` - Return a string representation
- `get_type()` - Return the runtime type name

# Example

```tml
class Person extends Object {
    name: Str

    override func to_string(this) -> Str {
        return "Person: " + this.name
    }
}

let p = Person { name: "Alice" }
print(p.to_string())  // "Person: Alice"
```
modules.summary: Object base class for TML's class hierarchy.

modules.name: profiler
modules.doc:
TML Native Profiler Module

Provides CPU profiling capabilities with output to `.cpuprofile` format,
compatible with Chrome DevTools, VS Code, and other profiling tools.

# Features

- **Manual profiling**: Control profiling start/stop and function tracking
- **Automatic instrumentation**: Use `--profile` compiler flag for automatic tracking
- **Chrome DevTools support**: Export format compatible with Chrome DevTools
- **Lightweight**: Minimal overhead when profiling is enabled

# Basic Usage

```tml
use std::profiler

func main() -> I32 {
    // Initialize and start profiling
    profiler::init("my_program.cpuprofile")
    profiler::start()

    // Your code here...
    do_work()

    // Stop and write profile
    profiler::stop()
    return 0
}
```

# Manual Function Tracking

For fine-grained control over which functions are profiled:

```tml
func do_work() {
    // Manual function entry/exit (optional - automatic with --profile flag)
    profiler::enter("do_work", "main.tml", 15)

    // ... work ...

    profiler::exit()
}
```

# Compiler Integration

Build with the `--profile` flag for automatic instrumentation:

```bash
tml build main.tml --profile
```

This automatically inserts profiling instrumentation into all functions.

# Output Format

The profiler generates CPU profile data in the `.cpuprofile` JSON format,
viewable in:
- Chrome DevTools (chrome://devtools)
- VS Code (using appropriate extension)
- Other tools supporting .cpuprofile format

items.name: init
items.doc:
Initialize the profiler with an output file path.

Call this before start() to set the output file.
Default output is "profile.cpuprofile" if not specified.

# Example
```
profiler::init("my_app.cpuprofile")
```
items.summary: Initialize the profiler with an output file path.

items.name: start
items.doc:
Start profiling.

Call this at the beginning of the section you want to profile.
Make sure to call init() first if you want a custom output path.

# Example
```
profiler::start()
// ... code to profile ...
profiler::stop()
```
items.summary: Start profiling.

items.name: stop
items.doc:
Stop profiling and write the output file.

This writes the .cpuprofile file to the path specified in init().
The profile can then be loaded in Chrome DevTools or VS Code.

# Example

```
profiler::stop()
// Profile written to disk
```

Pseudo-random number generation.

This module provides a fast PRNG ([`Rng`]) using the xoshiro256**
algorithm. `Rng::new()` seeds from the monotonic clock via SplitMix64
expansion for good entropy without requiring the crypto runtime.

# Example

```tml

var rng: Rng = Rng::new()
let n: I64 = rng.next_i64()
let r: I64 = rng.range(1, 100)
```

items.name: ThreadRng
items.doc:
A per-thread random number generator with high-entropy seeding.

`ThreadRng` wraps xoshiro256** but uses multiple entropy sources
(nanosecond clock + SplitMix64 mixing) to produce unpredictable seeds.
Each `ThreadRng::new()` call produces a differently-seeded generator.

For cryptographic security, use `std::crypto::random::SecureRandom`.

```tml
var rng: ThreadRng = ThreadRng::new()
let n: I64 = rng.next_i64()
let r: I64 = rng.range(1, 100)
```

modules.name: regex
modules.doc:
Simple regex engine using Thompson's NFA construction.

Supports:
- Literal characters
- `.` (any character)
- `*` (zero or more), `+` (one or more), `?` (zero or one)
- `|` (alternation)
- `()` (grouping)
- `[abc]`, `[a-z]`, `[^abc]` (character classes)
- `\d`, `\w`, `\s`, `\D`, `\W`, `\S` (shorthand classes)
- `^` (start anchor), `$` (end anchor)

# Example

```tml
use std::regex::Regex

let re: Regex = Regex::new("[0-9]+")
let matched: Bool = re.is_match("hello 42 world")
```

modules.name: channel
modules.doc:
Async bounded channel for inter-task communication.

Provides a bounded SPSC (single-producer, single-consumer) channel
backed by a circular buffer. Used for communication between async tasks.

# Examples

```tml
use std::runtime::channel::Channel

var ch = Channel::new(16, 8)  // capacity 16, item size 8 bytes
ch.close()
ch.destroy()
```

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
Async runtime for cooperative multitasking.

This module provides the async runtime infrastructure for TML's
async/await system, including an executor, timer, yield, and channels.

# Modules

| Module | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| [`executor`] | Single-threaded task executor |
| [`sleep`] | Timer and sleep operations |
| [`yield_now`] | Yield to other tasks |
| [`channel`] | Bounded async channel |

# Architecture

The async system uses a cooperative polling model:
1. Tasks are polled by the executor
2. If a task returns `Pending`, it's moved to the pending queue
3. When an event occurs (timer expires, data arrives), the task is woken
4. The executor polls the task again

# Examples

## Timer-based sleep

```tml
use std::runtime::sleep::TimerState

var timer = TimerState::new(100)  // 100ms
loop (true) {
    let result = timer.poll()
    if result.is_ready() { break }
}
```

modules.name: multi_executor
modules.doc:
Multi-threaded work-stealing task executor.

Provides a thread pool executor that distributes tasks across multiple
OS threads with work-stealing for load balancing.

# Architecture

The executor maintains:
- A **global queue** protected by a mutex for task submission
- A **shutdown flag** for graceful termination
- Worker threads spawned via raw OS thread API

# Task Model

Tasks are represented as `func(I64)` — a function taking a single I64
argument (which can encode a pointer to arbitrary user data). This avoids
generic closure limitations in the current compiler.

# Examples

```tml
use std::runtime::multi_executor::MultiExecutor

var exec = MultiExecutor::new(2)  // 2 worker threads

exec.submit(do(data: I64) {
    println("Task running with data: " + data.to_string())
}, 42)

// Start workers and process all tasks, then shut down
exec.run()
exec.destroy()
```

items.name: Task
items.doc:
A unit of work for the executor.

Each task holds a function pointer and an opaque I64 user data value.
The function is called with the user data when the task is executed.
items.summary: A unit of work for the executor.

items.name: MultiExecutor
items.doc:
A multi-threaded task executor with a global shared queue.

Workers pull tasks from the global queue and execute them. The executor
supports submitting tasks before or during execution, and graceful shutdown.

# Examples

```tml
use std::runtime::multi_executor::MultiExecutor

var exec = MultiExecutor::new(4)

exec.submit(do(data: I64) {
    println("Processing: " + data.to_string())
}, 100)

exec.run()
exec.destroy()
```
items.summary: A multi-threaded task executor with a global shared queue.

modules.name: bm25
modules.doc:
BM25 full-text search index.

Implements the Okapi BM25 ranking function for full-text search
with TF-IDF scoring. Supports multi-field documents with
configurable field boosts.

# Example

```tml
use std::search::bm25::Bm25Index

var idx = Bm25Index.create()
idx.add_text(0, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog")
idx.add_text(1, "hello world program example")
idx.add_text(2, "fox hunting in the wild forest")
idx.build()

let results = idx.search("fox", 10)
// results[0].doc_id = 0, results[0].score > 0
```

# Multi-field Documents

```tml
var idx = Bm25Index.create()
idx.add_document(0, "split", "pub func split(s: Str) -> List[Str]",
    "Splits a string by delimiter", "core::str")
idx.build()
let results = idx.search("split string", 5)
```

Indexes documents by tokenizing text into terms, computing inverse
document frequency (IDF), and scoring queries using the Okapi BM25
ranking function.

2. Add documents with `add_text()` or `add_document()`

- **k1** (default 1.2): Term frequency saturation. Higher values
  give more weight to term frequency.
- **b** (default 0.75): Document length normalization. 0.0 disables
  length normalization, 1.0 fully normalizes.

modules.name: distance

Vector distance and similarity functions.

Provides dot product, cosine similarity, euclidean distance, and
vector normalization for both F32 and F64 arrays. All functions
are pure TML using pointer intrinsics; LLVM auto-vectorizes the loops.

# F64 Functions

```tml

var a: [F64; 3] = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
var b: [F64; 3] = [4.0, 5.0, 6.0]
let dp = dot_product(&a[0], &b[0], 3)   // 32.0
```

```tml
var a: [F32; 3] = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
var b: [F32; 3] = [4.0, 5.0, 6.0]
let dp = dot_product_f32(&a[0], &b[0], 3)   // 32.0
```

modules.name: hnsw
modules.doc:
HNSW approximate nearest neighbor vector search.

Implements the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) algorithm
for fast approximate k-nearest neighbor search on high-dimensional
vectors. Also provides TF-IDF vectorization for converting text
to embeddings.

# Vector Search

```tml
use std::search::hnsw::HnswIndex

var index = HnswIndex.create(128)  // 128-dimensional vectors
index.set_params(16, 200, 50)      // M, ef_construction, ef_search

var vec: [F32; 128] = [0.0; 128]
// ... fill vec with embedding values ...
index.insert(0, &vec[0])

let results = index.search(&query[0], 10)  // Find 10 nearest
```

# Text-to-Vector Pipeline

```tml
use std::search::hnsw::{HnswIndex, TfIdfVectorizer}

// Build vocabulary from documents
var vectorizer = TfIdfVectorizer.create(256)
vectorizer.add_document(0, "quick brown fox jumps")
vectorizer.add_document(1, "hello world program")
vectorizer.build()

// Convert text to vectors and index
var index = HnswIndex.create(vectorizer.dims())
// vectorize + insert for each document
```

items.doc: A nearest neighbor search result from HNSW.
items.summary: A nearest neighbor search result from HNSW.

fields.doc:
The distance to the query vector (lower = more similar).
For cosine distance: 0.0 = identical, 2.0 = opposite.
fields.summary: The distance to the query vector (lower = more similar). For cosine distance: 0.0 = identical, 2.0 = opposite.

items.name: HnswIndex
items.doc:
HNSW approximate nearest neighbor index.

Builds a hierarchical navigable small world graph for fast
approximate k-nearest neighbor search. Uses cosine distance
(1 - cosine_similarity) as the distance metric.

## Parameters

- **M** (default 16): Maximum connections per node per layer.
  Higher M improves recall but increases memory and build time.
- **ef_construction** (default 200): Beam width during insertion.
  Higher values improve index quality but slow down build.
- **ef_search** (default 50): Beam width during query.
  Higher values improve recall but slow down search.

## Lifecycle

1. Create with `HnswIndex.create(dims)`
2. Optionally configure with `set_params(M, ef_construction, ef_search)`
3. Insert vectors with `insert(doc_id, embedding)`
4. Search with `search(query, k)` — no explicit build step needed
items.summary: HNSW approximate nearest neighbor index.

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
SQLite3 embedded database module.

Provides a safe TML interface to SQLite3, inspired by the Node.js `node:sqlite` API.

# Architecture

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`Database`] | Connection to an SQLite database file or in-memory DB |
| [`Statement`] | Compiled prepared statement with bind/step/column |
| [`Row`] | A single result row with typed column access |
| [`Value`] | Dynamic SQLite value (integer, float, text, null) |

# Examples

## Quick Start

```tml
use std::sqlite::{Database, Statement}

let db = Database::open_in_memory().unwrap()
db.exec("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, age INTEGER)")
db.exec("INSERT INTO users (name, age) VALUES ('Alice', 30)")
db.exec("INSERT INTO users (name, age) VALUES ('Bob', 25)")

let stmt = db.prepare("SELECT id, name, age FROM users ORDER BY id").unwrap()
loop (stmt.step()) {
    print("{}: {} (age {})\n", stmt.column_i64(0), stmt.column_str(1), stmt.column_i64(2))
}
stmt.finalize()
db.close()
```

## Prepared Statements with Parameters

```tml
let insert = db.prepare("INSERT INTO users (name, age) VALUES (?, ?)").unwrap()
insert.bind_str(1, "Charlie")
insert.bind_i64(2, 35)
insert.execute()

insert.reset()
insert.bind_str(1, "Diana")
insert.bind_i64(2, 28)
insert.execute()
insert.finalize()
```

## Transactions

```tml
db.begin()
db.exec("INSERT INTO users (name, age) VALUES ('Eve', 22)")
db.exec("INSERT INTO users (name, age) VALUES ('Frank', 40)")
db.commit()
```

modules.name: statement
modules.doc:
SQLite prepared statement.

The [`Statement`] type represents a compiled SQL statement.
It supports parameter binding, stepping through results,
and reading column values.

items.name: Statement
items.doc:
A compiled prepared SQL statement.

# Lifecycle

1. Create with `Database::prepare(sql)`
2. Bind parameters with `bind_*` methods (1-based index)
3. Execute with `step()` (returns true while rows available) or `run()`
4. Read columns with `column_*` methods (0-based index)
5. Call `reset()` to re-execute with new parameters
6. Call `finalize()` when done

# Examples

```tml
let stmt = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > ?").unwrap()
stmt.bind_i64(1, 25)
loop (stmt.step()) {
    print("{}\n", stmt.column_str(1))
}
stmt.finalize()
```
items.summary: A compiled prepared SQL statement.

modules.name: async_buffered
modules.doc:
Async buffered stream wrappers for efficient non-blocking I/O.

`AsyncBufReader` adds an internal byte buffer to any `AsyncRead` source,
enabling line-oriented reading and reducing the number of underlying
poll_read calls.

`AsyncBufWriter` batches writes and flushes when the buffer is full
or on explicit poll_flush. Reduces syscall overhead for small writes.

# Example

```tml
use std::stream::async_buffered::AsyncBufReader

var reader = AsyncBufReader::new(4096)
// Use with any AsyncRead source via poll_read_line, poll_fill_buf, etc.
reader.destroy()
```

A buffered wrapper that adds line-reading capability to any async source.

Maintains an internal byte buffer. When `poll_read_line()` is called, it
scans for `\n` (or `\r\n`) in the buffer. If not found, it polls the
underlying source for more data.

Unlike the synchronous `BufferedReader`, all read operations return
`Poll[...]` and may return `Pending` when the underlying source
would block.
items.summary: A buffered wrapper that adds line-reading capability to any async source.

items.name: AsyncRead
items.doc:
A non-blocking byte source that can be polled for readiness.

This is the async counterpart to `Readable`. Instead of blocking until
data is available, `poll_read` returns `Pending` when no data is ready
and arranges for the task to be woken when data arrives.

# Contract

- `poll_read()` fills the provided buffer with up to `buf.len()` bytes
- Returns `Poll::Ready(Ok(n))` with the number of bytes read
- Returns `Poll::Ready(Ok(0))` to signal end-of-stream (EOF)
- Returns `Poll::Ready(Err(e))` on I/O error
- Returns `Poll::Pending` when no data is available yet

When returning `Pending`, the implementation must arrange for the
task's waker (from `cx`) to be notified when data becomes available.
items.summary: A non-blocking byte source that can be polled for readiness.

methods.name: poll_read
methods.signature: func poll_read(mut this: mut ref This, cx: mut ref Context[Unit], buf: mut ref [U8]) -> Poll[Outcome[I64, IoError]]
methods.doc:
Attempt to read bytes from the source into `buf`.

Returns `Poll::Ready(Ok(n))` with the number of bytes read,
`Poll::Ready(Ok(0))` on EOF, `Poll::Ready(Err(e))` on error,
or `Poll::Pending` if no data is available yet.
methods.summary: Attempt to read bytes from the source into `buf`.

items.name: AsyncWrite
items.doc:
A non-blocking byte sink that can be polled for readiness.

This is the async counterpart to `Writable`. Instead of blocking until
the sink can accept data, `poll_write` returns `Pending` when the sink
is not ready.

# Contract

- `poll_write()` writes up to `buf.len()` bytes from the provided buffer
- Returns `Poll::Ready(Ok(n))` with the number of bytes written
- Returns `Poll::Ready(Err(e))` on I/O error
- Returns `Poll::Pending` when the sink cannot accept data yet
- `poll_flush()` ensures all buffered data reaches the underlying sink
- `poll_shutdown()` initiates a graceful shutdown of the sink

When returning `Pending`, the implementation must arrange for the
task's waker (from `cx`) to be notified when the sink becomes ready.
items.summary: A non-blocking byte sink that can be polled for readiness.

methods.name: poll_write
methods.signature: func poll_write(mut this: mut ref This, cx: mut ref Context[Unit], buf: ref [U8]) -> Poll[Outcome[I64, IoError]]
methods.doc:
Attempt to write bytes from `buf` into the sink.

Returns `Poll::Ready(Ok(n))` with the number of bytes written,
`Poll::Ready(Err(e))` on error, or `Poll::Pending` if the sink
cannot accept data yet.
methods.summary: Attempt to write bytes from `buf` into the sink.

methods.name: poll_flush
methods.signature: func poll_flush(mut this: mut ref This, cx: mut ref Context[Unit]) -> Poll[Outcome[Unit, IoError]]
methods.doc:
Attempt to flush all buffered data to the underlying destination.

For unbuffered sinks (e.g., raw TCP), this typically returns
`Poll::Ready(Ok(()))` immediately. For buffered sinks, this
forces all pending data to be written.
methods.summary: Attempt to flush all buffered data to the underlying destination.

methods.name: poll_shutdown
methods.signature: func poll_shutdown(mut this: mut ref This, cx: mut ref Context[Unit]) -> Poll[Outcome[Unit, IoError]]
methods.doc:
Attempt to shut down the sink gracefully.

This signals that no more data will be written. For TCP streams,
this sends a FIN packet. The shutdown may not complete immediately,
returning `Pending` if the shutdown handshake is still in progress.
methods.summary: Attempt to shut down the sink gracefully.

modules.name: buffered
modules.doc:
Buffered stream wrappers for efficient I/O.

`BufferedReader` adds an internal byte buffer to any readable source,
enabling line-oriented reading and reducing the number of underlying
read calls. Essential for parsing HTTP headers line-by-line.

`BufferedWriter` batches writes and flushes when the buffer is full
or on explicit flush. Reduces syscall overhead for small writes.

# Example

```tml
use std::stream::{ByteStream, BufferedReader}

var stream = ByteStream::from_string("line1\r\nline2\r\nline3\r\n")
var reader = BufferedReader::new(4096)
let line1 = reader.read_line(mut ref stream)!  // "line1"
let line2 = reader.read_line(mut ref stream)!  // "line2"
reader.destroy()
```
modules.summary: Buffered stream wrappers for efficient I/O.

items.name: BufferedReader
items.doc:
A buffered wrapper that adds line-reading capability to any source.

Maintains an internal byte buffer. When `read_line()` is called, it
scans for `\n` (or `\r\n`) in the buffer. If not found, it reads
more data from the source until a line delimiter is found or EOF.

# Memory Layout

```
Header (32 bytes at handle):
  offset 0:  buf_data (*Unit) — internal buffer memory
  offset 8:  buf_cap (I64)    — buffer capacity
  offset 16: buf_pos (I64)    — current scan position
  offset 24: buf_filled (I64) — bytes available in buffer
```

modules.name: byte_stream
modules.doc:
In-memory byte stream implementing both `Readable` and `Writable`.

`ByteStream` is a growable byte buffer with separate read and write
positions, making it ideal for testing stream-based APIs and for
constructing HTTP bodies in memory.

# Memory Layout

```
Header (32 bytes at handle):
  offset 0:  data (*Unit) — pointer to byte array
  offset 8:  len (I64)   — number of bytes written
  offset 16: capacity (I64) — allocated size
  offset 24: read_pos (I64) — current read position
```

# Example

```tml
use std::stream::{ByteStream, Readable, Writable}

// Write then read
var stream = ByteStream::new()
let data: [U8; 5] = [72 as U8, 101, 108, 108, 111]  // "Hello"
stream.write(ref data)!
stream.reset_read()

var buf: [U8; 5] = [0 as U8; 5]
let n = stream.read(mut ref buf)!   // n == 5
stream.destroy()
```

A `DuplexStream` combines a `ReadableStream` and a `WritableStream` into
a single bidirectional stream. Data written to the writable side is
independent of data pushed to the readable side.

This is the base for TCP sockets, WebSocket connections, and other
bidirectional channels.

also ends the readable side, and vice versa.

modules.name: mod
modules.doc:
Stream abstractions for byte-oriented I/O.

This module provides two layers of stream abstractions:

# Layer 1: Synchronous Behaviors (low-level)

| Behavior/Type | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| [`Readable`] | Byte source behavior — blocking `read()` |
| [`Writable`] | Byte sink behavior — blocking `write()` + `flush()` |
| [`ByteStream`] | In-memory read/write stream |
| [`BufferedReader`] | Line-reading and buffering for any source |
| [`BufferedWriter`] | Write buffering and auto-flush for any sink |
| [`pipe()`] | Copy bytes between synchronous streams |

# Layer 2: Event-Driven Streams (Node.js-style)

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| [`ReadableStream`] | Push-based readable with flowing/paused modes |
| [`WritableStream`] | Writable with backpressure, cork/uncork |
| [`DuplexStream`] | Bidirectional stream (read + write) |
| [`TransformStream`] | Transform data through a callback |
| [`PassThroughStream`] | Identity transform (pass data through) |

# Utilities

| Function | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| [`pipeline()`] | Chain readable to writable with error propagation |
| [`pipeline_transform()`] | Chain readable → transform → writable |
| [`finished_readable()`] | Wait for readable end/error/close |
| [`finished_writable()`] | Wait for writable finish/error/close |
| [`from_string()`] | Create a ReadableStream from a string |
| [`is_readable()`] | Check if a ReadableStream is readable |
| [`is_writable()`] | Check if a WritableStream is writable |

modules.name: passthrough
modules.doc:
PassThrough stream — identity transform.

A `PassThroughStream` passes all data written to its writable side
directly to its readable side without any transformation. Useful for
stream composition, testing, and as a simple buffer between producers
and consumers.

# Example

```tml
use std::stream::passthrough::PassThroughStream

var pt = PassThroughStream::new()
pt.write("hello")
let data: Str = pt.read(5)
assert_eq(data, "hello")
pt.destroy()
```

modules.name: readable
modules.doc:
Readable behavior for byte stream sources.

The `Readable` behavior is the fundamental abstraction for anything that
can produce bytes: sockets, files, in-memory buffers, decompressors, etc.

# Contract

- `read()` fills the provided buffer with up to `buf.len()` bytes
- Returns the number of bytes actually read (may be less than buffer size)
- Returns `0` to signal end-of-stream (EOF)
- Returns `Err(IoError)` on failure

# Example

```tml
use std::stream::{Readable, ByteStream}

var stream = ByteStream::from_string("hello world")
var buf: [U8; 5] = [0 as U8; 5]
let n = stream.read(mut ref buf)!   // n == 5, buf = "hello"
```
modules.summary: Readable behavior for byte stream sources.

A return of `0` indicates end-of-stream (EOF). Callers should stop
reading after receiving `0`.

modules.name: readable_stream
modules.doc:
Event-driven readable stream (Node.js-style).

`ReadableStream` is a push-based byte source that emits events when data
is available. It supports two modes:

- **Flowing mode**: Data is emitted via `"data"` events as soon as it arrives.
- **Paused mode**: Data accumulates in an internal buffer; call `read()` to pull.

# Events

| Event | Data | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `"data"` | Str pointer as I64 | Chunk of data available |
| `"end"` | 0 | No more data will be produced |
| `"error"` | Str pointer as I64 | An error occurred |
| `"close"` | 0 | Stream resources released |
| `"readable"` | 0 | Data available to pull (paused mode) |
| `"pause"` | 0 | Stream paused |
| `"resume"` | 0 | Stream resumed |

# Example

```tml
use std::stream::readable_stream::ReadableStream

func on_data(data: I64) {
    let chunk: Str = data as Str
    print("got: {chunk}\n")
}

var rs = ReadableStream::new()
rs.on("data", on_data as I64)   // Switches to flowing mode
rs.push("hello")                 // Emits "data" event
rs.push_eof()                    // Emits "end" event
rs.destroy()
```

modules.name: transform
modules.doc:
Transform stream — reads input, transforms it, pushes to output.

A `TransformStream` wraps a `DuplexStream`. Data written to the writable
side is passed through a user-provided `_transform` callback, which pushes
results to the readable side.

This is the base for compression, encryption, parsing, and other
data-transforming pipelines.

# Example

```tml
use std::stream::transform::TransformStream
use std::stream::duplex::DuplexStream

func my_transform(data: I64, duplex_ptr: I64) {
    let chunk: Str = data as Str
    let ds: mut ref DuplexStream = duplex_ptr as mut ref DuplexStream
    ds.push(chunk)
}

var ts = TransformStream::new()
ts.set_transform(my_transform as I64)
ts.write("hello")
let out: Str = ts.read(5)
ts.destroy()
```
modules.summary: Transform stream — reads input, transforms it, pushes to output.

modules.name: writable
modules.doc:
Writable behavior for byte stream sinks.

The `Writable` behavior is the fundamental abstraction for anything that
can consume bytes: sockets, files, in-memory buffers, compressors, etc.

# Contract

- `write()` writes up to `buf.len()` bytes from the provided buffer
- Returns the number of bytes actually written (may be less than buffer size)
- `flush()` ensures all buffered data reaches the underlying sink
- Returns `Err(IoError)` on failure

# Example

```tml
use std::stream::{Writable, ByteStream}

var stream = ByteStream::new()
let data: [U8; 5] = [72 as U8, 101, 108, 108, 111]  // "Hello"
let n = stream.write(ref data)!   // n == 5
stream.flush()!
```
modules.summary: Writable behavior for byte stream sinks.

modules.name: writable_stream
modules.doc:
Event-driven writable stream (Node.js-style).

`WritableStream` is a data sink that accepts bytes and emits events
for flow control. It supports:

- **Backpressure**: `write()` returns `false` when the internal buffer
  exceeds `highWaterMark`, signaling the producer to stop.
- **Drain**: The `"drain"` event fires when the buffer falls below
  `highWaterMark`, signaling the producer it's safe to resume.
- **Cork/Uncork**: Buffer multiple small writes and flush them together.

# Events

| Event | Data | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `"drain"` | 0 | Buffer below highWaterMark, safe to write |
| `"finish"` | 0 | All data flushed after end() |
| `"error"` | Str pointer as I64 | An error occurred |
| `"close"` | 0 | Stream resources released |
| `"pipe"` | ReadableStream ptr as I64 | A readable was piped to this |
| `"unpipe"` | ReadableStream ptr as I64 | A readable was unpiped |

# Example

```tml
use std::stream::writable_stream::WritableStream

func my_write(data: I64, cb: I64) {
    let chunk: Str = data as Str
    print("{chunk}")
    let callback: func(I64) = cb as func(I64)
    callback(0)  // signal success
}

var ws = WritableStream::new()
ws.set_write_fn(my_write as I64)
ws.write("hello")
ws.end()
ws.destroy()
```

modules.name: arc

items.name: Arc
items.doc:
A thread-safe reference-counted pointer.

`Arc` provides shared ownership of a value of type `T`, allocated on the
heap. Cloning an `Arc` produces a new pointer to the same allocation.
The allocation is deallocated when the last `Arc` is dropped.

Shared references in TML don't allow mutation. For mutable access,
use interior mutability patterns like `Arc[Mutex[T]]`.

# Thread Safety

Unlike `Rc`, `Arc` uses atomic operations for its reference counting,
making it safe to share across threads. The type `T` must be `Send + Sync`
to be shared between threads.

# Examples

```tml
use std::sync::Arc

let five = Arc::new(5)
let five2 = five.clone()

assert_eq(*five, 5)
assert_eq(Arc::strong_count(ref five), 2)
```
items.summary: A thread-safe reference-counted pointer.

methods.signature: func get_mut(this: mut ref Arc[T]) -> Maybe[mut ref T]

Makes a mutable reference into the `Arc`.

If there are other `Arc` or `Weak` pointers to the same allocation,
returns `Nothing`.

# Examples

```tml

when Arc::get_mut(ref mut x) {
    Just(m) => *m = 4,
    Nothing => unreachable()
}
```

methods.name: make_mut
methods.signature: func make_mut(this: mut ref Arc[T]) -> Maybe[mut ref T]
methods.doc:
Makes a mutable reference into the given `Arc`.

If there are other `Arc` pointers to the same allocation, then
`make_mut` will clone the inner value to a new allocation to
ensure unique ownership. This is also referred to as clone-on-write.

If there are no other `Arc` pointers (strong_count == 1),
the inner value is returned directly without cloning.

See also `get_mut`, which will fail rather than cloning.

# Examples

```tml
use std::sync::Arc

let mut data = Arc::new(5)
*Arc::make_mut(mut ref data) = 42
assert_eq(*data, 42)
```

items.name: Weak
items.doc:
A weak reference to an `Arc[T]`.

Weak references don't keep the data alive. When all strong references
are dropped, the data is dropped (even if weak references remain).

Use `Weak::upgrade` to try to get a strong reference. It returns
`Nothing` if the data has already been dropped.

# Examples

```tml
use std::sync::Arc

let five = Arc::new(5)
let weak_five = Arc::downgrade(ref five)

when weak_five.upgrade() {
    Just(strong) => assert_eq(*strong, 5),
    Nothing => panic("dropped too soon"),
}

drop(five)  // Drop the only strong reference

assert(weak_five.upgrade().is_nothing())
```
items.summary: A weak reference to an `Arc[T]`.

methods.doc:

Calling `upgrade` on the result will always return `Nothing`.

```tml

assert(empty.upgrade().is_nothing())
```

modules.name: async_mutex
modules.doc:
Asynchronous mutual exclusion primitive.

This module provides [`AsyncMutex[T]`], a mutex that yields to the async
executor instead of blocking the thread when contended. This makes it
suitable for use in async contexts where blocking would starve other tasks.

# Overview

Unlike the synchronous [`Mutex[T]`][super::mutex::Mutex], `AsyncMutex[T]`
does not block the operating system thread when the lock is held by another
task. Instead, it spins briefly and then yields control back to the executor,
allowing other async tasks to make progress.

# When to Use

- Use `AsyncMutex[T]` when protecting shared data in async code
- Use [`Mutex[T]`][super::mutex::Mutex] when in synchronous code or when
  the critical section is very short (no I/O)

# Examples

## Basic Usage

```tml
use sync::async_mutex::AsyncMutex

let counter = AsyncMutex::new(0)

// Acquire lock (spins + yields if contended)
{
    let mut guard = counter.lock()
    *guard = *guard + 1
}  // guard dropped, lock released
```

## Try Lock (Non-blocking)

```tml
use sync::async_mutex::AsyncMutex

let mutex = AsyncMutex::new(42)

when mutex.try_lock() {
    Just(guard) => print(*guard),
    Nothing => print("lock held"),
}
```
